subtopic: USE OF WATER FROM NIAGARA RIVER FOR HYDROELECTRIC POWER PURPOSES

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: USE OF WATER FROM NIAGARA RIVER FOR HYDROELECTRIC POWER PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to table three copies in English and three copies in French of the Niagara diversion treaty, which is being signed in Washington this afternoon by the Canadian ambassador, Mr. Hume Wrong, and by the United States Secretary of State, Mr. Dean Acheson. With your permission I should like to make a short statement on this treaty.
We have been discussing with the United States government the possibility of amending article 5 of the Boundary Waters treaty of 1909 with respect to the use of water from the Niagara river for the generation of hydroelectric power. In these talks we have had the valuable assistance of the chairman of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario and the chairman of the Niagara parks commission. The discussions have resulted in a Niagara diversion treaty.
The Boundary Waters treaty of 1909 authorized the diversion by the United States of 20,000 cubic feet of water per second, and the diversion by Canada of 36,000 cubic feet per second. Although Canada was thus allowed to use more water than the United States the power produced by the extra Canadian share has been exported to the United States. As a result, each country has had the use of hydroelectric power produced by approximately half of the water made available by the 1909 treaty.
During the second world war, additional diversions of 13,000 cubic feet per second on the Canadian side and 12,500 cubic feet per second on the United States side were authorized on a temporary basis.
The new Niagara treaty reserves adequate quantities of water for flow over the falls and through the rapids, and then authorizes the use of all remaining water for power
purposes. Since this water will for the first time be divided equally between the two countries, the United States government is being informed through our embassy in Washington that when facilities have been constructed in the United States to use the full United States share of water, Canadian export licences then in effect will not be renewed unless circumstances existing in Canada at that time make such a course desirable.
It is not possible to say just how much more water this treaty will make available to Canada, since the necessity of preserving the scenic beauty of the falls and rapids is the first charge on the fluctuating volume of water in the Niagara river. However, it is expected that both countries will normally have the use of more water than before. At the same time, the fact that the temporary arrangements agreed upon during the war are being superseded by a permanent agreement will permit the construction of new power plants of the latest design to replace a number of existing plants now in operation which cannot make the most effective use of the available water. For these two reasons, a substantial increase in the amount of hydroelectric power generated at Niagara can be expected once this treaty has been ratified and the new power plants have been constructed.
Nevertheless the demand for power keeps increasing, and this additional Niagara power cannot be expected to meet the full needs of Ontario and New York state. The power requirements of these areas can be met only by the full development of the potential power of the St. Lawrence river. The additional Niagara power should help to tide us over the period required for the construction of the St. Lawrence facilities, but the need for St. Lawrence power is as urgent as it ever has been. The new Niagara diversion treaty does not in any way lessen Canada's interest in, and desire for, early ratification by both governments of the St. Lawrence waterway and power agreement of 1941.
The treaty contains two provisions designed to protect and enhance the scenic beauty of the Niagara river and falls. It calls for early completion of remedial works to ensure an unbroken Crestline on the falls by distributing the waters more evenly. It also ensures that the flow over the falls and through the rapids will not be reduced below the amounts

Niagara Diversion Treaty which experience has shown are essential for the preservation of the full scenic spectacle.
I have been advised by the chairman of the Hydro Electric Power Commission of Ontario that this treaty meets with the approval of the premier of Ontario, the Ontario hydro, and the Niagara parks commission.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: USE OF WATER FROM NIAGARA RIVER FOR HYDROELECTRIC POWER PURPOSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I feel sure that every hon. member of this house will welcome the statement which has been made with regard to the treaty which is being signed today, not only because it will provide more power for one part of this country, but because of the convincing evidence it offers of the friendly and effective association between Canada and the United States in enterprises of this kind.
I feel sure that everyone will welcome also the statement of the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) to the effect that this will in no way be allowed to obscure the immense importance of proceeding with the power development of the St. Lawrence river. This treaty will provide an additional supply of water which, with certain new developments in power plant construction, will be of great help; but at a time when Canada and the United States are looking to the protection of the peace which is the main concern of people generally throughout the free world, I believe it is right to say that there could be no more cogent evidence of an effective working partnership between two countries than the fact that an agreement could be reached for power development of the St. Lawrence, which would add so much to the potential resources of both countries for peace or for any situation that might arise.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to table a copy of an order in council passed on February 23 under the provisions of the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act, transferring, effective as of January 18, 1950, the powers, duties and functions vested in the Minister of Finance under the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation Act to the Minister of Resources and Development, as was contemplated by the statute setting up the Department of Resources and Development.
The law officers of the crown tell us that, a former transfer having been made from the

Minister of Finance to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply, whose department ceased to exist when the new department came into being, it is necessary now to have an order in council transferring these functions from the Minister of Finance to the minister of the new department.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question, for the purpose of clarification only. A moment ago the Prime Minister announced that the Minister of Finance has divested himself of certain responsibilities by transferring them to the Minister of Resources and Development, and that prior to that time he had divested himself of those responsibilities by the same method. How can the Minister of Finance transfer to another minister something he has already transferred from himself to that minister? Simple addition would indicate that he had nothing left to transfer after he had done his first job.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION ACT
speechtext: That was our impression when the statute substituting the new department for the old department was passed, but the law officers of the crown have given the opinion that the order in council which was passed transferring certain duties from the Minister of Finance to the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply ceased to have any effect when the statute under which that department was constituted was repealed. The opinion was that it would be necessary to have a new order in council passed to vest these powers and functions in the minister of the new department. Their opinion evidently was that upon the repeal of the statute setting up the ministry of reconstruction and supply the order in council ceased to have effect, and that the powers and functions reverted to the minister who had first been vested with them by parliament.

subtopic: CENTRAL MORTGAGE AND HOUSING CORPORATION ACT
speechtext: In other words, there is no intestacy among departments of government.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. A. Blanchette (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of National Defence
subtopic: TRANSFER OF ARMY PERSONNEL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 22 last the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Ferguson) asked the following question, which is to be found at page 128 of Hansard:
In view of the fact that soldiers belonging to the permanent army must obey orders and move where they are directed, and there are men in the ranks with families moving to Ottawa, is any provision being made for the housing of these men, or must they continue to seek any shelter they can possibly obtain and pay exorbitant prices? Is any attempt being made to provide dwellings for these people?
In answer thereto I should' like to say that the policy of the Department of National Defence is to press forward with the construction of married quarters in more isolated centres. At Rockcliffe, however, because of the number of service personnel employed, 108 houses have already been erected; 200 more are in the course of construction or under contract, and it is expected that contracts for a further 300 units will be placed this year. In addition, the policy is adopted of earmarking some of the houses erected by the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation in larger centres for service personnel. A large proportion of married service personnel are also veterans and have access to accommodation for veterans. More married quarters in proportion to numbers of personnel have been provided in Canada than in any other country.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Pending the decision of parliament on Bill No. 2,


which proposes the abolition of capital punishment', I should like to ask the Solicitor General whether the government will consider suspending executions in Canada, including those scheduled to take place in Vancouver tomorrow morning.

subtopic: REQUEST FOR SUSPENSION OF PENDING EXECUTIONS
speechtext:
The hon. member was kind enough to give me notice of his question. In reply may I be permitted to say that although proposals to abolish capital punishment have been before this house on previous occasions, we have no departmental record of any request' such as that advanced by my hon. friend having been considered in the past.
As the hon. member knows, the administration of justice throughout Canada is in the hands of the provincial authorities; and according to practice the postponements of executions are matters to be considered upon their merits by the courts of the province under section 1063 of the Criminal Code. It is felt that to act upon a mere legislative proposal as though it were a statutory enactment could hardly be justified. To suspend executions in Canada, as requested by the hon. member, in my estimation would be an improper and unprecedented intervention by the federal executive authority under the law as it stands and as it must' be applied throughout Canada unless and until it is changed by parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, living in a democracy as we do, we appreciate the opportunity of taking part in

the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Even if it were not customary to congratulate you again on having been elected as Speaker of this house, we should still want to do so, because we feel that while everything may not be all right in the world, with your wisdom and guidance everything is all right in this House of Commons.
I should like also to congratulate the mover of the address, particularly since he is one of us from Saskatchewan. We appreciate the fact that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) chose an up-and-coming young man from Saskatchewan to present this motion. We all hope that the ability of the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) will become more generally recognized, and that in future he will have the opportunity to be of even greater service to his country.
All who heard the hon. member for Ville-neuve (Mr. Dumas) second the motion for the address must have marvelled at his ability to express himself in both languages. As time goes on we hope to be able to do something ourselves in that direction, and reciprocate the kindness French-speaking members have always shown by addressing themselves to us in English when they know we do not understand their mother tongue. The people of Villeneuve also have every right to be proud of their member.
At the same time I should like to congratulate the new minister and the new parliamentary assistants. The people in Maple Creek who have come from other parts of the dominion I know would want me to ask every hon. member to take their greetings back to the places from which they originally came, in almost every part of Canada.
For a few moments 1 should like to speak about my constituency. Situated in the southwest part of Saskatchewan, it is one of the largest in the settled portion of Canada. If one were to travel every road allowance that has been surveyed in Maple Creek, he would travel one and a half times around the world. It is in the Palliser triangle, which is an area extending from a point in north central Saskatchewan, catching a corner of Manitoba and running on down in a southwesterly direction into Alberta. When it has rainfall it has great production, but unfortunately it experiences dry spells which bring extreme crop failure. This is another of those years during which the people of that area are suffering extremely, not only from drought conditions but also from one of the most severe winters in history.
It is difficult for anyone in this or any other country who has never gone through
The Address-Mr. Studer the experience to comprehend what it means to have no crop. We may have marketing and other difficulties, but when a man is without a crop of any kind of course he lacks the wherewithal to sustain himself, he receives no return for his work of a year or perhaps a series of years, and is unable to carry on. The people in that area who have had no income for years are hoping that both provincial and federal governments will see that this spring they are enabled to carry on and make the contribution to the country that they are able to make when they have good crops. We should do everything possible to assist those people who, against great odds and with the utmost difficulty, have remained in that country, hoping against hope eventually to make their contribution to the well-being of the country. I believe it would be a great help if payments to the farmers this spring under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act were made equal in purchasing power to the payments made in 1939, when the act was brought into operation. I do not think that is asking too much, if by doing so we can place these people in a position to carry on and plant another crop without being in debt before the seed is even in the soil.
It is not my intention to dwell on this point at great length. Not all is gloom and despair even in that area, however. Maple Creek has the best beef in Canada. I have been told by those who should know that if you want a good steak you should go to Maple Creek, where the restaurants serve the best steaks in Canada. My constituency also has some of the best sheep in this country; it has the best light horses; it has the best wheat, with the highest protein content in Canada. It has the best, or almost the best, light honey, as witness what happened to the exhibits from Valmarie and Maple Creek this past fall at the Canadian national exhibition. It has the best water because the king and queen were served with this Shaunavon water during their western trip. In the Cypress Hills it has a provincial park. There is one lake, Lac Pelletier, and that is where I live. It has some of the best educational institutions, at Gravelbourg and other places. In common with the other constituencies in the land it has, without a shadow of a doubt, the best people in the world.
Today this area comes under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act, which has been administered by the dominion government. As time goes on it will be found this area is equal to any other area coming under the operation of the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. When the operations of this act are
252	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Studer finally completed, no one will be standing in this house asking for assistance to the people of my area. We want to look after ourselves; we do not want to be beggars all our lives. We want to have a chance to make our living as the remainder of the people do, and to be equal with all the other people in this Dominion of Canada. I hope that in 1950 the dominion and the province will cooperate in making farming possible in this area, as well as in other areas similarly situated.
I noticed, Mr. Speaker, that there was an amendment and subamendment to the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I believe one part of the amendment called for the elimination of the means test in respect of old age pensions. I believe that everyone in this country, regardless of party, is in favour of the elimination of the means test. If it is to be eliminated and there is not sufficient money available to carry the additional burden of old age pensions, what particular social service could those who moved the amendment offer to reduce the burden of providing additional pensions for the aged? There is only one way of carrying old age pensions without a means test, and that is to increase production. I would suggest to the mover of that amendment that he do everything possible to see that production is increased throughout the length and breadth of Canada, because it is only through increased production that wealth can be made available to pay for the increased social services. If these people desire to be of service to the aged and blind of Canada, and all the others who are in need of assistance, then they can go through this country preaching increased production.
If it is necessary to work an eight-hour day to accomplish that result, well and good. If it takes a nine-hour day, I suggest they recommend that the people work a nine-hour day. If it takes a ten-hour day, they could recommend that the people work ten hours. On the other hand they may wish to recommend that the people follow the example of the farmers and work sixteen hours a day; and no one may be hurt in the process.
From the terms of the amendment, one would think that the aged of this country were in a pitiable condition. It has been suggested that the means test is the meanest test. Can anyone name any other country in the world, under any form of government, that has a better system of old age pensions, or more deductible income in the calculation of income? If so, I wish he would name it. Let us help the aged and the blind, but let us not consider that Canada has been doing something which would not compare favourably with what is being done in any other


country. Which country would they care to uphold to us? Time and again during the last session reference was made to England, New Zealand and Australia, as examples that we should follow. So far this session I have not heard a single reference to those countries. Previously it was said that everything Canada should do should be patterned after what was happening in those countries. None of them, however, can meet what Canada has done in the way of social services. Every country in the world has a means test. If there is one which has not, I wish some hon. member would name it. When the means test is removed, Canada will be the first country in the whole world to remove it.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, I believe the mover of the amendment was a former premier of Ontario, while the mover of the subamendment, I understand, is leader of a party which has a government out in Saskatchewan with which he would like us to become intimately acquainted, or possibly even adopt. It seems to me that when members in this House of Commons advocate what should be done, they should have at least set an example in their own particular province, over which, at some time or other, they may have had some control, directly or indirectly. In the province of Ontario, the richest province in the Dominion of Canada, we find no supplementary payment for the aged. In Ontario, however, there is a mothers' allowance. Among the needy people in the world there are those who, through some unfortunate circumstance, have lost the breadwinner of the family. In Ontario these mothers' allowances are paid, but with a means test. I suggest that some people should start practising what they preach before they come into the House of Commons and tell us what to do.
Furthermore, out in the province of Saskatchewan, in spite of what happens in Ontario, the old age pensioners receive a supplementary payment of $2.50, but only after a means test. This was set up by a socialist government. It is necessary to undergo a means test before even this sum of $2.50 is paid. The province of Alberta pays $7.50 as a supplementary payment, without a means test. In British Columbia there is a supplementary payment of $10, without a means test. The socialist members from Saskatchewan have been preaching the elimination of the means test, yet there is a means test in that province before the old age pensioners receive that low supplementary payment.
The province of Saskatchewan also pays a mothers' allowance with a means test. It is the lowest mothers' allowance payment made by any province in Canada. These members from Saskatchewan, therefore, must be

talking with their tongues in their cheeks when they come before this House of Commons and try to tell us that they are the only people who have any regard for the rest of the people in Canada.
Again I would say that, when such a subamendment is put forward, those who favour it should practise what they preach. Let us all work together to make it possible for the aged and blind to receive adequate compensation. Let us find ways and means of increasing production, so that the wealth will be available to enable Canada to be the first country to remove the means test.
I believe the subamendment said that the government had failed to take adequate measures to protect civil liberties, and at the same time to curb espionage and other harmful activities of communists and fascists in Canada. If I recall aright, three or four years ago something happened in regard to espionage in Canada. As I recall it, there were some people in the socialist group who, either directly or indirectly, pleaded for the spies who were arrested and brought up for trial. If I do not remember correctly, I suggest that hon. members look at page 5742 of Hansard of August 31, 1946, and see what the present minister of health in the Saskatchewan government said about the fellows who were arrested for espionage in Canada; at that time he was the member for Swift Current. Read what he said, and then revert back to this subamendment which suggests that the government has not taken adequate measures to curb espionage in Canada. If it were possible for me to move another subamendment, it would read like this: That the government failed to take adequate measures to protect the civil liberties and at the same time to curb espionage and other harmful activities of communists, fascists and, I would add, socialists in Canada. I will not say that they are the same; I will only say that they are related. Blood is thicker than water. Some of the things that are in fascism are in socialism, and some of the things that are in both are in communism. They are therefore related. As someone so kindly told me yesterday, the farther you are from socialism, the farther you are from communism. I think that is true.
In any event, I heard some explanations from some of those over on the socialist benches last session, and there was an indication of it this year in which they tried to tell us that they were not communists, if I remember correctly. My thought on the matter is this. Why speak about not being a communist if you are not one, or if you have no association with them? Why talk about it at all? One thing I have not heard in this House of Commons is a corking good
The Address-Mr. Studer speech against communism by any of those socialists over in the far corner of the house. I suggest that they can all talk on that subject and make real speeches on the evils of communism. They are certainly the people to do so, because there is not a single subject that has ever been brought before this House of Commons on which they have not been able to give an opinion. I have listened to their profound, pontifical and infallible pronouncements for quite a number of days, and certainly they would be the people to do justice to a good speech against communism.
I noticed that the leader of the socialists over in that far corner was telling us the other day what bred communism and fascism. I ask him what breeds socialism; and if it is not exactly the same thing, I will take back everything I have said. No matter where you look around the world, socialism is out of date and is passing out of the picture; and if there are any people living in this Dominion of Canada who have nothing better than socialism to offer, I think they had better go back to their studies, go through all the history of the world and find out all the causes of everything, including the causes of war; because irrespective of what hon. members over there have been talking about, I hope to have the opportunity some time to show this House of Commons that an "ism" practised somewhere in the world-and that includes the last ten years-has been the cause of every war that we have had. Socialism is out of date. The socialists preach about the benefits of socialism. Where has it ever been in existence long enough for anyone to know whether it is good, bad or indifferent? It does not last. It passes out of the picture, because as soon as people see what it is based on, they begin to find ways and means of discarding it as rapidly as they possibly can. It is something that does not stay fixed. It is like this hybrid wheat that the scientists have produced; they take a parent of one wheat and a parent of another wheat, and cross them. They work for years trying to develop a new variety of wheat. One of their greatest troubles is to have that wheat remain fixed. After a variety is established and reseeded, it reverts to the variety of the one parent or the-other. Difficulties have been experienced with this hybrid wheat, just as difficulties have been experienced with hybrid corn in the United States. It does not reseed itself. You always have to go back and get hybrid corn. It is the same way with socialism; it does not stay fixed. We have heard some talk about unemployment, and we have heard reasons advanced for it; we have been told that some of it is seasonal, some perhaps otherwise. But if there is one thing that the people of this country should guard against, in my opinion, unemployment certainly is that thing. If there is any anguish in the heart of the father of a family in this country who is denied the right to earn daily bread for his family, it may have unhappy results. I repeat what has been said by many others, that hunger will drive people to do almost anything in an effort to sustain the children who are dependent upon them. Therefore I would advise government, whether it is the government I support or any other one throughout the length and breadth of this country, to let no condition appear anywhere that causes suffering, hardship, privation and the anguish that is in the hearts of those who are not permitted to earn their daily bread. No democratic government anywhere in the world can afford to let a condition such as that exist. The only countries that can afford to do so are the totalitarian countries, the dictatorship countries; because they can take their unemployed and put them in the army or put them in a camp. We do not do that in the democratic countries.
So I say that if you eliminate the causes that give concern and anxiety to the people of this country, you will not have very much to worry about. Every resource of every province should be utilized to eliminate this condition, if it exists-and we have been told that it does; otherwise in the future there will not be any resources there to use.
I believe I heard some talk about employment on farms. We sometimes hear people talking about the movement of farmers to the

We have the eight-hour day, the forty-hour week, and two weeks' vacation with pay for our labouring people-and that is a good thing; I want the labouring people to have the best of everv-thing; I want them to have all the purchasing power that it is possible for them to have, because as a farmer I want a place to sell my goods, and if labour has no purchasing power -and it is the biggest consumer in Canada- my goods will not be sold. So I want them to have everything they can possibly have that will increase their health, their consuming capacity, and their enjoyment of life. But if labour can maintain a good standard of living by working eight hours a day and forty hours a week, how long are we to expect the farm boys and their fathers to work from twelve to sixteen hours a day and not have a standard of living equal to that of the labouring people with their eight-hour day system?
In my view one of the greatest difficulties facing Canada today is that people have been drawn away from the farms. The time will come when people may have to go hungry either in this or in other countries. Therefore we have to bring those people back to the farms and improve farm conditions. We have to modernize them and create a love of the soil, something which is missing in this country today. Only love of the soil will enable the farmers to nurture it and to give it the care it needs to keep it from eroding. They must adopt a system of rotation, and care for the soil as they would care for members of their families.
That is what love of the soil means. But it is fast disappearing from this country. So if there is anything any of us can do to keep the importance of farming before the people of this country, and the importance of the growing of food, we shall have accomplished something, we shall have made a contribution to the welfare of our country.
Farming is a way of life-a way I would not exchange for any other way of life. But it is a way of life which many people are exchanging for a substance which they think is a reality, to be found in other forms in the cities and elsewhere. Let us remember that there has never been any record in the history of any country of their having a too prosperous agriculture. There has never been any danger of that; let us keep that in mind, over and above many other things which are not of such great importance.
Many of us in the House of Commons and out Saskatchewan way have been giving a considerable amount of thought and have been pondering ways and means of alleviating conditions, not only in the drought areas

The missionaries who went through that land seventy-five or a hundred years ago came back with reports about it and gave advice to governments of that day as to what they thought, based on the information they had gained and what they had learned from the first settlers, the Indians, about what the country could support in the future. They indicated what in their opinion would be the proper number of people to be allowed to take up land out there, and they made suggestions as to what the government could do about it. Because of difficulties, particularly freight rate difficulties, we are not able to dispose of as much of that oil as we would like to. Freight rate discrimination would perhaps be a better phrase to use. The eight per cent sales tax was removed last session and up to that time that was just another discrimination. This question of freight rate discrimination has been brought to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). I hope in the near future they will take the necessary action to see that this oil field is further developed.
Because of the present shortage of coal the further production of this oil is doubly necessary and the freight rate discrimination should be removed. When passenger train service was curtailed, the oil people at Lloyd-minster offered to give the C.N.R. oil free of charge for the operation of the train service between Edmonton and Saskatoon, but the railroad did not find it possible to accept that offer. Along with many other sections of the country we are still faced with a curtailed train service. I am not going to discuss this matter any further at this time, but I do hope that the coal shortage will soon be relieved and our train service fully restored.
The Prime Minister went on to deal with old age pensions and devoted a lot of time to that subject. We have on the order paper a resolution to set up a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons to investigate pension schemes in other countries and possibly make some recommendations. I suggest that before this committee makes its report-I do not expect it will be made until perhaps the next election-we should do something to relieve the distress of certain older people at the present time.
Not long ago an amendment to the Old Age Pensions Act was passed providing for an increase of $10 per month, but we failed, perhaps intentionally, to increase the amount of allowable income. At the present time the allowable income for a single pensioner is $600 and for married pensioners, $1,080. In order to have given all these people that $10 increase we should have provided for an increase of $10 per month in the allowable income. Because that was not done many of these people have been denied the benefits of the $10 increase.

In certain cases, perhaps not many, people are denied pensions because they cannot furnish proof of age. Several methods of proving age can be adopted. A birth certificate may be presented, a marriage certificate or the date of joining some organization. However, many people from Europe have entered this country, sometimes coming here in a hurry. Because of what is to us a peculiar spelling of a name other branches of the government are not able to find any record of these people having entered Canada. As a result they are denied a pension because they are unable to furnish proof of age. I have had such cases myself, and I expect that other hon. members have had similar experiences. Where no other proof of age can be found I suggest that the individual be brought either before a medical doctor, who should at least have some knowledge of age, or perhaps before the old age pensions board for the particular province in which the prospective pensioner resides.
In my opinion-and I think it is admitted by every fair-minded person-the present pension of $40 a month is not sufficient to keep our old age pensioners. Like all other Social Crediters, I believe we should have a minimum of at least $50 per month, and that the age at which the pension is payable should be reduced from where it is at the present time because many of our people, particularly those working in industry and on farms, reach the end of their working days long before they attain the age of sixty. I think unemployment figures will show that when people reach a certain age they are not wanted any more. Employers just do not want them. Where are these old people going to get work? During their lifetime they have contributed their share to the building up of the country, and the country should now see to it that they are provided with a pension that will keep them in reasonable comfort during their old age.
At the last session the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. Mclvor) made a suggestion that the sales tax be removed on hearing aids for old age pensioners. We fully endorse his suggestion, and I would add to it dental and optical equipment. The prices of these things are certainly far too high at the present time and we should be able to afford the loss of the eight per cent tax on these articles. Then we have another class of people to whom I referred at the last session, and to whom I hope to refer again later on, the physically incapacitated. Many of us who are in possession of all our faculties, mental and physical, find it difficult to make a living, and these people who are physically incapacitated through no fault of their own are finding it pretty hard to get along. Their families are responsible for their care, and I believe the government 55946-18a
The Address-Mr. Fair could go a long way towards helping them out. I hope before the session ends legislation will be introduced as to that matter, providing pensions at least equal to old age pensions.
Turning to agriculture, I feel that in the past many people have not given the industry the consideration to which it is entitled. I have here an editorial to be found in the Rural Co-operator of January 24, 1950, a publication printed in Toronto. It refers to a speech by Louis Bromfield, novelist, farmer and internationally famous conservationist, to the Ontario crop improvement association, and reads:
A "more detestable man never lived than Hitler", he said, "yet Hitler did utter one truth. He said Germany was fighting because it didn't have enough living room and it didn't have enough to eat. That was the true cause of the last two great wars. Naziism was only the political manifestation of that profound economic cause."
The editorial goes on to say:
If we accept that explanation, and many will, we are at once faced with the question: What are we doing today to make sure that no people in the world shall ever again have that cause or excuse for going to war? Is reduced farm production, in terms of international relations, a practical policy to follow? Could not any country with a farm surplus better afford to give it all away at any expense than run the risk of a further conflict with all its staggering cost in money and lives?
In connection with giving away food, I have figures taken from the Alberta wheat pool budget of February 10, 1950, showing that the United States commodity credit corporation on November 30,	1949, had
$3,370,190,000 invested in price support loans or in commodities held. Perhaps that is something we might consider. I have other excerpts from articles that I should like to read for the purpose of building up the case for agriculture. The- next one is a report of an address by Mr. C. H. Millard, also to be found in the Rural Co-operator of January 24. The heading of the article is:
Labor Doesn't Allow for Any Hitch-hikers.
In addressing the Ontario federation of agriculture, Mr. Millard, a director of the United Steel Workers of America, had this to say:
We don't allow for hitch-hikers in the union. Every member must pay his way. We have learned that you must not go about formulating policies unless you are prepared to pay the cost.
Then the article goes on to read:
Mr. Millard, one of the best known labour leaders in Canada, had been invited to tell "Labour's story" to the farm people at the convention.
He stated further:
"Our first objective is to unite all labour people. When we started in at the job of organizing we found the workers badly disunited. They were disunited on the basis of religion, race, fraternity and

The Address-Mr. Fair social barriers. Our next objective was to engage ourselves, with our employers, in the art and process of collective bargaining to ensure an adequate standard of living and good working conditions. Our third objective," said Mr. Millard, "is to win social security for ourselves and our families and to seek to bring about ever higher standards of living." Labour, he said, felt that action on the economic front was not sufficient. Political and legislative action was also necessary if many problems were to be overcome. "We face grave political problems having a bearing on economic problems, particularly in matters of trade."
He went on to say:
Frankly, I am little concerned over the loose thinking of the past few years about the markets for our so-called exportable surpluses. . . . The standard of life everywhere must be raised, here in Canada as well as abroad, so that labour is able to buy the goods the farmer produces, and the farmer can buy ours.
I hope that will be taken into account by many people who have to deal with labour and agricultural policies. To the farm organizations of Canada I would say that it is important that every farmer belong to a farm organization. I would also go a little further and say that it is important for every farmer to attend the meetings of the organizations, particularly those where policy is laid down. It is important that farmers elect the right leaders, and that they see to it day in and day out, week in and week out, year in and year out that those leaders follow a sound and progressive policy on behalf of the organizations. If that is not done, then we may be led down a road that is not good for farmers, for labourers, or for Canada as a whole. That is a warning I have given to farmers before, and I am giving it again today in the hope that farmers all across Canada will benefit from it. I am not saying that as one who is on the outside because, since coming to Canada in 1914, I have had quite a little to do with farmers' organizations.
I also have a report of an address by Mr. Hannam, president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, speaking before the Ontario federation meeting in Toronto on January 12, 1950. The article reads in part:
"Feeding the world is an international task and must be approached on an international basis," he stated. Farmers in all countries want to remove the needless risks and insecurity in the agricultural industry of the old order; farmers in all countries want to produce for * a known market with a reasonable measure of stability, he said. "More than ever before our price stability in Canada is dependent on price stability in the world market," Mr. Hannam told the delegates.
Then it goes on:
"If Canada had been buying more goods from the United Kingdom during the past few months we would not be having trouble with U.K. food contracts now," Mr. Hannam stated.
"We have tariffs against British woven woollen products, clothing made from wool, boots and shoes,

washing machines and bicycles, to name only a few, and these tariffs are one good reason why there are not more U.K. goods coming into this country."
Then he said that this type of tariff was a subsidy to industry and that farmers should not be criticized for seeking protection for farm products through price supports. I am not going to read any more of Mr. Hannam's statement, but I have something here by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner). I am glad he is in his seat at the moment, looking happy; and I hope he continues to do his best for the farmers, as he has done in the past. I was pleased to learn that he has no opposition in the cabinet to his agricultural policies, because many people were quite satisfied that the minister would have been able to do better but for some opposition in the cabinet. The statement recently made gives us the assurance that there is no such opposition, and I hope that is correct. Speaking at the Niagara Falls convention on February 1 the minister is reported as follows:	.
Mr. Gardiner said the government has no intention of going into the business of buying and selling, although it proposes to put price support legislation on a permanent basis at the next session of parliament.
However, he added, he is going to do everything he can to get trade contracts without utilizing funds from the price support legislation of $200 million, which he felt certain would be voted again without difficulty.
Meanwhile he suggested farmers set up strong cooperatives and distributing agencies in the marketing of produce throughout the provinces.
And a little later:
While it was a tribute to his department that farmers apparently felt pleased at the distribution of food products under emergency conditions during the war-
I might' interject that while they were satisfied with the distribution they were not satisfied with the financial return.
-those conditions no longer applied. The job no longer could be done from Ottawa.
The minister said he also wished to dispel rumours that he is meeting opposition from the cabinet in his efforts on behalf of the farmers.
Mr. Gardiner said farmers cannot expect floor prices to be set at the highest level prevailing during the last three years. In most cases, the price was set about 10 per cent lower than the highest level.
Then apparently he went out' to Alberta, that province where the sun shines all the time, and at a meeting in Lethbridge had this to say:
"During the last year, or year and a half in some cases, we have been asking all consumers in Canada to make up to the farmer for what he lost during our price controls . . .
"We have no difficult surpluses with any of our farm products. We are not in the period yet when we should feel down in the dumps on farm prices."
Mr. Gardiner declared that the only way farmers could succeed in the west, or in all Canada, was to produce to the limit of their capacities the farm

products which they could best produce, especially for the domestic market. Until Britain reached its objective, possibly at the beginning of 1952, of accumulating $2 billion in dollar credits so she could restore her trading to normal levels, Canadian farmers must put their operations on a sound basis. When Britain could again trade freely the Canadian farmer, he felt sure, would be able to compete successfully against any country in the world for British markets.
I think that will serve as a foundation for what I propose to say a little later. When I came to this country thirty-six years ago I remember that the farmers worked anywhere from ten to sixteen hours a day, and even longer during some of the busier seasons. At the same time organized labour was working fifty to fifty-five hours a week. Today we find the farmers still working the long hours they worked then, while organized labour in many cases has brought down the work week to forty-four hours, and is now seeking a further reduction to forty hours. In my opinion that is not too bad. At the same time the farmers have no guaranteed pensions, and no guarantee of any kind if the weather is not kind to them; they have no holidays with pay. Today organized labour has its pension schemes; it has holidays with pay; and in most cases the workers have better homes than the farmers, with electric lights, bathtubs, electric washing machines and things like that. I say to labour it is a good thing they have those things, because the country can produce them and through their organizations they have been able to obtain those benefits for themselves. But what about the farmer; does he have all those conveniences and those guarantees of security? He has not. Many people blame the farmer for the high cost of living. In the Manitoba Co-operator of January 5 I saw a short sentence which may give us an idea of what brings about the high cost of living:
On Friday, December 30, retail price of No. 1 back bacon was 98 cents per pound at three Winnipeg retail stores, and 77 cents per pound wholesale. The bacon comes wrapped in one-half pound and one pound packages, ready for sale over the counter, for which the retailer takes 21 cents per pound as his mark-up, or 27-3 per cent. The same is true of some other prepared meats. A quick serve whole ham retailed at 67 cents for which the wholesale price was 47 cents, or a mark-up of 42'5 per cent. A regular ham retailed at 60 cents, the wholesale price being 39 cents, a mark-up of 53-8 per cent.
These things contribute to the high cost of living. In many cases the farmer had nothing whatever to do with it, because during the peak prices he was getting 36 cents a pound for Wiltshire sides. That was not live weight; that was dressed, delivered at the seaboard.
In the past we have had many contracts with Britain. Only a few months ago the Minister of Agriculture and some of the other ministers told us we would not be able to renew those contracts. Since those
. The Address-Mr. Fair reports were circulated in the press and over the radio there has been a great deal of discontent among our farmers; but we are told that by some good luck or in some way contracts have been entered into again this year for certain quantities of bacon and cheese. They could not renew the egg contract; I guess the British people are getting their supplies somewhere else. In spite of all the statements that have been made by the cabinet ministers I feel that we have suffered a definite loss in our markets in Britain. I have here the report of a speech made by the Minister of Agriculture to the Canadian chamber of commerce in London in December, 1948. I should like to read part of it, because I think it gives his attitude toward our dollar system and other things as well. Speaking of the 1949 contracts he said:
I am not making these statements to be critical of the United Kingdom government or its agents.
I am making them to impress upon you the fact that the British people want our bacon, want our eggs, want our beef, want our wheat. I am making them to impress upon you that if dollar requirements had not intervened we would have been in a position to send you in 1949 over 300,000,000 pounds of bacon, nearly 200,000,000 pounds of beef,
80.000.	000 dozen of eggs, several hundred thousand barrels of apples, thousands of bushels of beans and much jam, none of which your traders feel you can afford to have from us because of the dollar shortage. We cannot sell the apples, beans, jam and salmon to anyone at any price under the present dollar arrangements and for the moment we are finding it impossible to dispose of millions of bushels of linseed at 30 per cent less than you are paying others for it.
They are taking 140,000,000 bushels of wheat and
50.000.	000 pounds of cheese from us because they must have them and we appear willing to provide them for fewer dollars than any other will supply them.
All this is bringing me to wonder if an unknown economist, or was it an Abraham Lincoln or some such individual as Churchill, was not right when he said: 'That he would rather have the money in his pocket tied to the unthinking inanimate substance called gold which cannot change its mind than to the manipulations of some small group of crackpots who fancy themselves as economists or statesmen.'
The minister never told us to whom he was referring, but I should like him to tell us whether he was not referring to those economists they have in the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada. I think I am right in suggesting that those are the crackpots to whom he had reference.
Further along in his statement, he said:
I am not convinced that this latter statement is correct, but I am convinced that the world is not in any state of mind where it can be expected to agree that the manipulation of any system or systems of currency is going to be allowed to interfere with the will of those who have emptjr stomachs when it is preventing surpluses of food to get to them. It might be a good thing for everybody if they would close down the United Nations; meetings long enough to permit of the United Kingdom and United States experts getting together and settling some basis upon which dollars and

The Address-Mr. Fair , sterling can be converted to allow nations like Canada to produce food to feed the starving millions and distribute it. If that cannot be done then they might provide some means by which we can have an opportunity to fill our country with working people to develop the resources the world needs for its war and other machines, that they may eat the surpluses already piling up but which we are not permitted to sell.
I see that my time is slipping away, so instead of dealing with the world organization as I intended, I shall refer members to the speech made by the member for Acadia (Mr. Quelch) on Thursday last, in which he dealt with the whole matter. At that time he showed that the money experts or crackpots had misled the delegates to the meeting of the world organization which considered a plan for the distribution of food. Today we are not allowed to supply that food to the hungry people of the world.
One day last week the member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) contradicted a statement made by the member for Souris (Mr. Ross), when he said that during recent years agriculture had suffered a loss of $2 billion because of government policy. I am not sure that I am prepared to go as far as that because I have not calculated the loss. I can say, however, that for the years 1946, 1947 and 1948 the farmers' loss on wheat sales alone amounts to slightly more than $508 million. If the hon. member for Yorkton wishes to challenge that statement, we shall see about it. I have the government figures to bear out what I say. As a result of the losses the farmers have suffered since the outbreak of war, and because of certain things that were done owing to the war, I am suggesting that the support prices be fixed at the 1949 level for a couple of years at least. I do feel that is not an extravagant request, because during that ten-year period since war broke out the farmers have paid rather expensive insurance premiums to guarantee themselves those prices in the future.
As I have said before, the industries receive subsidies by way of tariff protection. There is no reason in the world why farmers should work approximately twice as many hours as the people in other occupations, and have a much lower standard of living in most cases, yet be refused price support. I feel that at the present time, or any time for that matter, there is no need for gloom among the people of Canada, provided their affairs are properly administered. It may mean we shall have to have another government in order to ensure that proper administration. If it is necessary, let us have that change. Last year, I believe we had a national production of approximately $16 billion. Last week we were told that it is expected the national production for 1950 will amount to $16,250 million. We are not

working to the limit, by any means, as will be seen from the figures on unemployment that have been recited in this house during the past two weeks. If those people were put to work, production could be increased to a great extent. I feel that the farmers of Canada have done their share of the producing, and they want to know now what the government is going to do about its share. As I said before, if the government is not equal to the job, then let us dismiss the government, and dismiss these crackpot money experts in its service. We Social Crediters have a policy that will, to a large extent, eliminate the difficulties in this and many other countries.
Since the wheat board legislation terminates at the end of July, I believe some legislation should be brought in at this session to continue the operation of the wheat board. I would suggest that, by legislation or some other means, the grain exchange should be eliminated before it has another chance of starving many of the unsuspecting farmers of the western provinces. The grain exchange has had its day, and has brought much misery. I want the government to take effective measures, by legislation or otherwise, to rid the country of this scourge of pests.
Social Credit has got a policy, not only for agriculture but for other industries as well. For agriculture we propose, first, a home market constantly supplied with purchasing power. Many people claim that is not necessary, that we should just let things continue as they are. People will continue buying until they have used their money, and then, if they want to go hungry, that is up to them. Many people, however, are not able to find better jobs. If purchasing power were assured, you would not have the troublesome surpluses that have been built up in some parts of Canada even today.
The second point is a compensating price discount technique for ensuring fair prices to producers without causing inflation. Number three is a two-price system to work in conjunction with an international commodity clearing house to guarantee parity returns to farmers. Number four, extension of export markets and acceptance of nonconvertible sterling as a means of recapturing and retaining British and European markets. Number five, provincial-dominion producer marketing boards to serve as a foundation for Number 6, a permanent Agricultural Prices Support Act. Floor prices should be established at a level which would enable farmers to get along.
I see that my time has expired, so I shall discuss many of the other subjects I had in mind as the days of the session go by.

speechtext:
May
I first, Mr. Speaker, congratulate the mover (Mr. Larson) and seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. This has become a customary opening for those who rise in this debate. I wish to assure them that the sentiments are none the less sincere, because they have performed their task well. They have shown that they have ability as well as good training for the office they now occupy.
I wish to congratulate the Prime Minister upon his choice of the gentleman who now occupies the post of Minister of Immigration and Citizenship (Mr. Harris). It must be gratifying to the minister to see how well his appointment was received by members of all parties in this house. He is a man of ability and judgment, and it is to be hoped that he will not fall prey to the fantastic plans of those who would open wide the doors of our country and even finance the admission fee at a time when we are experiencing in certain regions of the country temporary difficulties in finding employment for those who were born in Canada or who have been here for a considerable time. In a country such as ours, immigration is an important topic, and although I do not join with those who believe we should not let anybody in, I think our policies in the matter should be carefully weighed and that we should not forget that the timing of a measure is often as important as its provisions. I feel quite sure, however, that with the first Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) we may expect all the guarantees and the caution that a man of his judgment and intellect would consider advisable in the matter.
While I am distributing congratulations, I think it might be in order also to congratulate the government, and especially the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), on proposing the appointment of a committee to examine and study the best possible method to ensure security.
A moment or so ago the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe), in his speech, objected to that method and said that the government had made promises but instead of fulfilling them was just appointing a committee. I cannot see what is wrong in setting up a committee. It is the democratic way to act, for the government to give to all parties in the house an opportunity to study a question before a bill is brought before the house. We oftentimes complain that we are faced with a measure without members having a chance to express their views before the government has already committed itself, sometimes even-in detail, to a given proposal. I think the government is to be congratulated on taking the steps it is now taking. Unless there is a
The Address-Mr. Picard change in the motion, however, I must express deep regret that the government has not seen fit to heed the pleas and requests made by many hon. members and in which I have repeatedly joined the hon. member for Terrebonne (Mr. Bertrand), that consideration be given to the possibility of setting up a system of pensions for invalids. For a number of years the hon. member for Terrebonne has proposed a resolution to this effect, and he has done so again this year. His resolution is on today's order paper and reads as follows:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should during the present session take into consideration the advisability of including in their social security program a system of allowances to every person, without any sufficient income or means of support, who, by reason of an injury, accident, congenital infirmity or incurable disease, is at a disadvantage in seeking or obtaining employment, or incapable of providing for his subsistence, and whose age prevents him from benefiting by the social security legislation now in force.
On a number of occasions I have spoken on a resolution of that nature or one in nearly similar terms, not only because of the knowledge I have of conditions in my own constituency but because, from year to year, each time that I rose in my place I have received a flood of correspondence from all over the province, or from those parts which had been reached by the press which reported my speech. From those letters I have learned of the sad situation of so many unfortunate people. In a speech a year or so ago, by -comparison with countries in which such plans exist, I established -that the amount necessary to cover such a pension scheme would not be exaggerated. Today, however, I have other subjects to deal with, and I shall not go any further in the matter than to ask the Minister of National Health and Welfare to consider the advisability of widening the scope of the reference to the committee so that, at the same time that it considers the question of old age pensions, it may consider pensions for invalids.
There are rumours that there might be in the offing a conference between the federal and provincial health authorities on the question of aid to incurable persons. I wonder if that includes a scheme of pensions for incurables. If that is so, it is all to the good. Even if such- a conference is planned, I do not see why an opportunity should not be given to the members of this house, at the same time as they discuss the question of old age pensions, to express their views on the question of pensions for invalids. This question has *been brought here time and again. As I said a moment ago, the sad plight of these people cannot be overlooked and cannot, for much longer, be left without special consideration by the government.

The Address-Mr. Picard
Many countries now have such schemes. In some of them they are contributory; in others they are just outright pensions such as we have here up to this moment for the old people. But be it one way or the other, either outright pensions as we have now for the aged or a contributory system, with special allowance or special provisions for those who are born invalid, and never had any occupation of any sort, something should be done but it might be made contributory for those who have an occupation and later become invalid.
As it is one minute to six, Mr. Speaker, and I am about to change the subject of my remarks, I should like to call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at eight o'clock.
