speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, loyalty to those who have made it possible for me to stay in this house for the last ten years, loyalty to those who remained loyal to me at the last general election despite, I might say, the venomous attacks of my opponents, prompts me to devote much of my attention to the future of Canadian agriculture. Eighty-five per cent of my constituents toil and sweat on the land to get from it their daily subsistence, and that of their families. I make my concern the fate of these men and women who, for the great part, toil on the farms, work on the farms handed down from generation to generation in the same families or who, as the younger sons of such families, have ventured into the forests and wrested from nature that lot of land that will become the fertile patrimony of their sons and grandsons.
This is why time and again during these last years I have tried here to explain the point of view of the Quebec farmer. That is why I have endeavoured to understand their problems and to make suggestions which I have thought would produce beneficial results for them. I have never known personally their hardships. I cannot say I have ever shared their tasks, nor can I claim to have an actual or even an indirect experience of their difficulties. But as they kindly accepted me in 1940, as one of them, to speak in their name in this House of Commons, and as they have twice since then renewed the expression of their confidence in me, it is natural that I should devote a considerable part of my activity to the study of the conditions, local, national and international, which may affect their welfare.
I feel it my duty, for these reasons, to express here some of these thoughts which have resulted from the consideration I have


given to the fate of Canadian agriculture as regards especially the necessity of finding markets for our agricultural surpluses.
One of the most important matters affecting the economic life of our country at the present time is the marketing of these surpluses of our agricultural products, both as to prices obtainable and the quantities for which we might find buyers. The situation as it stands today is discreetly mentioned in the speech from the throne in the following words:
Circumstances outside Canada have been responsible for some downward adjustment in the price of farm products.
And later:
Continued difficulties arising out of the worldwide dollar shortage have resulted recently in reduced purchases of a number of our export products.
These two apparently innocuous statements refer to a problem much vaster and of much greater consequence to our economy than these guarded words may indicate. The whole of our agricultural development and much of our national progress hinges on the successful disposal at reasonable prices of our food surpluses. Not only as a representative of a rural constituency, but from a firm conviction that the well-being of the country is dependent upon the healthy condition of our agriculture, I feel it my duty to devote my time tonight to a consideration of these problems and of the possible remedies to be applied.
Before looking into what the problem has in store for us, it would not be fair not to outline, even if briefly, what has been the result of the government's agricultural policy over the last few years. This afternoon the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) spoke about low prices. Can he find at any time under any administration by his party such prices as we have had under a Liberal administration for the last few years? I do not have to go even as far as the war years which, admittedly, have been years most profitable to Canadian farmers in general. But we have figures for the four years following the war, from 1946 to 1949, for the five products upon which agriculture generally depends for its prosperity-wheat, hogs, cattle, milk and eggs.
In this connection I should like to quote from an address delivered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) to the annual meeting of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture on January 31 last-and I would ask hon. members opposite to take note of these figures, because they are official. On that occasion the minister said:
During the four years since the war we have marketed on an average 90 million bushels of wheat.

more per annum than in the four years before the war, which is approximately one-third more. During the four years since the war we have marketed on an average 345 million pounds more pork per annum than in the four years before the war, which is approximately one-half more. During the four years since the war we have marketed 370 million pounds more of beef per annum than in the four years before the war, which is above one-half more. During the four years since the war we have marketed two billion pounds more milk per annum than in the four years before the war, which is one-eighth more. During the four years since the war we have marketed 150 million dozen more eggs per annum than in the four years before the war, which is more than 60 per cent more.
Prices on those five products will average at least 65 per cent higher. The difference is best represented in the gross farm income in the last four-year period compared with the preceding period. The average annual total for the last four years is $2,133 million and for the previous period $650 million.
For the benefit of those who prefer the net income figures they are, for the last period $1,305 million and for the previous period $435 million. The gross income or the net income is more than three times in the last four-year period what it was in the four-year period before the war. It would appear that it will continue at that average for at least another year, and thus give us the best five years in our experience.
There is no way in which the pessimists can figure us into depression or difficulties up to the present.
Mr. Speaker, let us now see the situation as it is today. That was the situation up to that moment. Let us see what it is now. Again I quote from the same address by the Minister of Agriculture:
At the end of 1949 the three most important contracts are still in existence. The bacon contract continues so far as delivery to the British is concerned for the entire year of 1950, but so far as guaranteed returns to the farmer is concerned, until July 1, 1950.
Under it the government agrees to take delivery of A Wiltshire sides at $32.50 a hundred and to deliver to Britain 60 million pounds at $29 a hundred. If the plan works as intended the farmer is assured a floor price for hogs approximately 2 cents a pound more than we are obtaining for what goes to Britain. This means that the farmer will get about one-tenth of the return over and above the British price from the treasury of Canada, and the other nine-tenths directly from the consumer. $29 a hundred is $2 a hundred more than we received in 1947. It is more than we have received in any year excepting 1948 and 1949.
The farmer has been netting more for some months, under this plan, than he could have obtained in any other way. His price will still be higher than I have been able to find farmers getting in any country, except Britain. These higher returns have been justified because at an earlier time he is presumed to have taken less than he might have secured.
The wheat and cheese contracts are still in existence. The wheat contract ends July 31, 1950.
We are now negotiating.
The cheese contract has been renewed for one year at five cents a pound less than from April 1, 1948, to December 31, 1949, but it is the same price as was received in 1947 and five cents a pound
The Address-Mr. Picard more than in any year before 1947. The government has subsidized the price by three cents a pound and pays in addition a premium of one' cent on 93 score and two cents on 94 score cheese.
As far as eggs are concerned, the minister has suggested that we cannot hope to sell eggs in any form to the United Kingdom in 1950. The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) suggested that the markets were lost. I cannot find from those figures that the markets are lost. I shall come in a moment to the remedies that might be applied to this situation as it may develop. I should like to quote again the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner), who said on December 14:
In the meantime we will be trying to tide you over the year 1950 with an agreement on cheese which we think we can negotiate and one on bacon to cover the remainder of the 1949-50 natural hog year which we have hopes of being able to negotiate.
Then on January 31, 1950, the minister said:
What about the future of the British market? It is still taking approximately $400 million worth of our farm products and therefore is our best outside market. The prospects are that it will continue to be our best market. If they take all our surplus cheese and 120,000,000 bushels or more of our wheat, they will continue to be, if not our best market, one we cannot afford to be without. Any effort farmers have made to remain in it is worth continuing. We are only going to lose $30 million in 1950 from the British market as compared with what we had in 1949 if we lose all we were asking for and did not get.
The present contracts which we have for commodities other than wheat are as follows: 60,000,000 pounds of bacon with a seaboard value of approximately $17 million. The cheese contract may vary with a possible maximum of approximately 85,000,000 pounds of a value of around $21 million f.o.b. Montreal. That is far from the gloomy picture we got this afternoon from the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. We now have covered the * situation as we see it, and as to its causes I cannot find any better words than those contained in an article published in the National Review of October, 1949, entitled, "Canada and the sterling area", by the Right Hon. L. S. Amery. Speaking of Canada he says:
Her economy is, like ours, essentially a highly unbalanced one. It is one of immense surplus productive capacity in respect of foodstuffs, raw materials and minerals. However great her industrial development-and she is destined to be one of the world's great industrial powers-the immense area of her agricultural lands and, even more perhaps, the vast and scarcely tapped mineral resources of the great pre-Cambrian rock shield that covers half her territory, will make it a matter of generations before she can absorb anything like the whole of her vast primary output. On the other hand her economy is a deficiency economy, temporarily in some elements of industrial equipment, but permanently in respect of all the products of the

The Address-Mr. Picard
southern temperate, sub-tropical and tropical regions. External trade is for her, as for us, both a matter of existence and the essential condition for the fullest expansion of her resources.
It is an oft-repeated fact that we must buy much of what we need in the dollar area and sell most of our surpluses in the sterling area. Most of our surpluses are food products. Although the problem is national in scope, first and above all it affects the Canadian farmer. On this subject I again quote the Minister of Agriculture in an address delivered at the fifth session of the food and agricultural organization conference held in Washington on November 24, 1949, when he said:
Thus, in relation to some other exporting countries Canada has an economy which is particularly dependent upon exports-both from the point of view of the volume and the consequent reaction of Canadian prices to changes in world prices.
And again:
It is essential for us to export 75 per cent of our wheat. Unless our exports can be maintained we cannot continue to purchase large quantities of goods from the United States and the United Kingdom. We should purchase from other countries, including those two, such goods as they can produce at lower costs than they can be produced in Canada.
And again:
The importance of agricultural exports in our economy places Canada in a unique position. Products of farm origin, while below wartime levels, still represent a substantial part of total exports, and of these wheat alone accounts for about 15 per cent. Canadian farmers, therefore, are still vitally concerned with world markets and are fearful lest monetary difficulties and other trade obstructions deny them entry to their natural market which is the market of Great Britain. We are the nearest of all countries which supplied them in wartime. We still want to supply them until their needs are satisfied. If we did that we would not have any marketing problem in those products which they required from us during the war.
I agree with what the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said this afternoon that the British market ought to be cultivated. What I cannot understand is why he complains that prices for wheat were fixed during the war. I cannot understand why one of the leaders of the Tory party is objecting to what was done in the hope of keeping the British markets after the war and helping Great Britain during the war. He has talked much this afternoon about the speeches made during the campaign by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Minister of Agriculture. He touched upon almost everything except the North Star, which was made such an issue by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) during the campaign. I cannot help but think of the success that crowned the efforts of the government and I think the same thing will be true one day of the efforts of the Minister of Agriculture in attempting to solve this situation.
With regard to the reasons for the shrinkage last year in our exports to Great Britain the minister made a statement which brings me to the next part of my remarks. He said:
This was not because the United Kingdom did not want our cheese-and many of our other products- but because she did not have the dollars to pay for it. If we could remove the one difficulty of lack of dollars we would have solved many of our problems.
As to the remedy, the minister stated that it would be threefold. First, he referred to the fact that we have lent Great Britain $1,250 million, the expenditure of which was intended to be spread over until 1952; second, we are encouraging purchases in Great Britain for dollars; and, third, we are discouraging the purchase of some commodities from the United States.
I shall try to demonstrate in the third part of my remarks that there is another field which the government does not seem to have explored. I shall come to that in a moment, but first I should like to make a last quotation from the remarks of the Minister of Agriculture. I may be accused of quoting the minister too often, but 1 admit that I have a weakness for him. Of all the experts in agriculture in Canada he is the one who has most consistently been right in the past and is the one upon whom we can most depend in the future.
Politics aside, I am deeply convinced that Canada has been most fortunate in having as Minister of Agriculture for the past 15 years a man who was so qualified to direct its agricultural policies. The minister has weathered many storms and he has met with outstanding success. He is not the type of man who seeks praise nor does he like empty compliments, but I think in all justice and equity it is appropriate to recognize his outstanding ability and the eminent services he has rendered, both to his country since he has been in office and to the allied cause during the last conflict.
Although the foregoing has been truly said without any political intent, I may add that the fact that he is one of the true Liberals in this house and in the cabinet far from detracts from the personal admiration I have for him.
To get back to the subject of my remarks, I wish to repeat my last quotation of the minister.
If we could remove the one difficulty of lack of dollars on the part of Britain we would have solved many of our problems.
This seems to be substantiated by the conditions prevailing during the war when we supplied the United Kingdom with the necessary amount of dollars to secure in Canada what was needed in the way of food and armament. Let us examine therefore the summary of balance of payments transactions between

Canada and the sterling area, mainly the United Kingdom, from 1940 to 1945. We find that total current expenditures in Canada on account of the sterling area amounted to the fantastic sum of $10,430 million. The expenditure of such vast amounts has evidently boosted the Canadian economy and accounts for much of the wartime prosperity for those six years. Sales of food products to Great Britain amounted to $2,290 million. To facilitate an understanding of my argument, I ask the consent of the house to include at this point in Hansard a short summary of the balance of payments above mentioned as taken from page 38 of the Canadian Balance of International Payments, 1926 to 1948.

The hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) said that we should do as much as we can to help Great Britain get the necessary dollars to buy more of our products. I hope he will agree with the proposal I am about to make which will show that she can get the dollars for that purpose. In 1939 British investments in Canada amounted to $2,476 million, and in 1947, the last year for which I could get figures, they stood at $1,642 million. I have already outlined, when I spoke on the mutual aid bill on May 11, 1943, that the so-called repatriation of Canadian National Railways bonds was just a shifting of figures from private shareholders to the Canadian government, but at the time I advocated that we should avail ourselves of a provision contained in the mutual aid bill which read:
That the governor in council may determine the terms and conditions upon which such war supplies

The Address-Mr. Picard are made available to any of the united nations and may require in certain cases payment or repayment in kind or property or reciprocal action or provision of supplies or other direct or indirect benefit as may be deemed appropriate.
I held at the time that Great Britain should buy all the Canadian securities held in that country and turn them over to the Canadian government. This was no extraordinary procedure. It had been followed as to United States securities held in Great Britain and in that regard I wish to quote from a report published in the Federal Reserve Bulletin reading as follows:
At the beginning of the war, in August, 1939, the British owned about $950 million worth of United States securities.
Summarizing the balance of the quotation, between that time and the end of 1940 they had liquidated $334 million, and of the remaining $616 million $389 million were either sold or were pledged to the reconstruction finance corporation against loans that government corporation made to Great Britain during the period January-August, 1941. Another $60 million were held to be pledged with the reconstruction finance corporation at September 1, 1941. This left $167 million in securities which had not been repatriated between that time and the end of 1943.
The same thing was done by Great Britain as regards Argentine securities held in Great Britain. I was not the only one to advocate that at the time. The Financial Post on September 30, 1939, had foreseen the move as inevitable. It even quoted from a government statement dated September, 1939, which ended with the following words:
In the first instance Canada's assistance in supplying food and ammunition to Great Britain will probably involve repatriation of Canadian securities held in London and, at a later stage, the granting of credits.
That was in September, 1939, more than ten years ago, but there are still $1,642 million of Canadian securities held in Great Britain on which we paid during the six years of the war $357 million, and on which we were still paying in 1947 $53 million per annum. However, credits and even gifts were granted before repatriation was asked for. It is evident that some financial experts have changed their minds between the first declaration of the government and the time when the policies were definitely established.
Yet had we then acted as the United States and the Argentine did, we would be one step further in the logical solution of our railway problems, which were mentioned this afternoon by my friend from Dufferin-Simcoe, since the government would have acquired free of charge the control of the Canadian Pacific Railway which we are letting drift into United States hands. In 1937 54-89 per


cent of the common or ordinary shares of the Canadian Pacific Railway, representing $175 million, were held in Great Britain as well as 95-09 per cent of the preferred stock, $133 million, and at least $285 million of the company's bonds. If in return for our gifts of $3 billion Great Britain had acquired and transferred the C.P.R. securities amounting to $593 million, she would have had still to thank us, and the first step in the solution of our railway problem would have been made at no further cost to the treasury, a substantial improvement over what was done in the days of the Canadian Northern and the Grand Trunk railway.
Even if there is no excuse for not repatriating these securities during the' war, the opportunity is still there of using this $1,642 million to good advantage. Here comes my suggestion to help solve our marketing problem. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said:
If we could remove the one difficulty of lack of dollars . . . we would have solved many of our problems.
This afternoon the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said, "Let us help Great Britain get the dollars". To this I answer that Great Britain has a potential fund of over one and a half billion dollars to purchase Canadian goods which, distributed over a period of years, would ensure Great Britain of her necessary supplies and Canada of her necessary market.
Before examining a method of effecting an orderly repatriation of these securities it may be worth while to investigate the nature of these values. I will just give an outline of what they are. Canadian bonds held in Great Britain in 1946, mainly government and municipal, amounted to $105 million; railways and utilities, $315 million; corporations, $97 million; common stock holdings amounted to $675 million, most of which was in railway issues. The balance of $357 million represented British direct investments in Canadian branches, subsidiaries and other companies controlled in the United Kingdom.
The technique of such a repatriation can easily be established by the Bank of Canada and the foreign exchange control board. The British government knows where these securities are. They have been registered, and they might actually buy them at a price equivalent to their market values. Owners might receive all or part of the purchase price by way of sterling bonds. The securities could then be handed to the Bank of Canada which, with the foreign exchange control board, has facilities for their orderly liquidation on the Canadian market. Some of them could even be sold on the United States

The Address-Mr. Picard
market if necessary. Some may say that in this way the ownership of more of our industries would pass to the United States. I do not see that we would be any worse off than if these securities remained in Britain; at any rate the same result is achieved by the private sale of Canadian securities by the British on the United States market, although with the proviso that each time a security is sold it is credited to the British account here in repayment of the loans already made.
No better example could be found than that of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which I mentioned a moment ago. In 1937, as I said before, Britain held 54-89 per cent of the ordinary shares of that company while the United States held 22-22 per cent. According to the 1949 report of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the last report we have, as of December 31, 1948, Britain held only 37-49 per cent of the stock of the company, which meant that these securities had been disposed of privately. At the same time, however, the United States held 43-41 per cent of the stock. Thus control of the Canadian Pacific Railway, instead of having been given to us outright, now is passing into United States hands. If any such liquidation had been part of a marketing deal at least we would have derived some benefit from the transaction.
Furthermore, having control of the Canadian Pacific pass into United States hands might very well have a considerable repercussion on the finances of the Canadian National. What if a powerful United States empire, such as was built a few years ago by Robert Young of the Chesapeake and Ohio, obtained control of the Canadian Pacific? Such a company could immediately route most of its Canadian business through its Canadian subsidiary, or to be more exact the Canadian company it controlled. It is not to be forgotten that seventy years ago the Canadian Pacific received about as much in the way of subsidies as the companies that now constitute the Canadian National. At that time the company obtained from the government vast areas of land, of which a large proportion still appears to be their property. This might be an added incentive for the country to regain control of the railway, rather than see outside interests profit by the accrued values of such lands, particularly in Alberta.
This afternoon the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) put the question: How can we sell to the British if they have no dollars? Well, here is a source of dollars which I suggest to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) and the hon. member. Of course the main question remains: if there
were no dollar shortage, how much more would the British buy from us? The reason given the public for the curtailment of some of the contracts is the lack of dollars, but it might well be that the matter of price is an equally important factor, since it has been customary for Britain in time of peace to be a tough bargainer, to forget the interests of the commonwealth at large and to think only of herself. This afternoon the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said, "Don't sell the British commonwealth short". I have here an article from New Zealand which says "Britain is turning back to the empire".- Well, the British act like real businessmen and drive a hard bargain, while we are sentimentalists. I do not blame them for that either. During the war we went so far as to give our wheat to Britain for less than we could have obtained for it elsewhere. That was another sacrifice we made in the hope of gaining the gratitude of Britain and keeping those markets after the war. Most of what we have done, and most of the negotiations the minister has carried on, had as their ultimate aim the retention of those same markets following the war.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I hold that we cannot overlook any method which may facilitate the marketing of our agricultural surpluses. Britain appears to be a natural market; in that I agree with the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. It is a natural market, but it is increasingly restricting its purchases from us, and Britain will continue to be a tough trader in the years to come. The difference between Britain and Canada is that Britain has the practical sense of doing business in a businesslike way, of fighting wars to ensure either her supremacy or her survival. On the other hand we are sentimentalists, who fought wars in the past more because of the attachment of some of our citizens to their former mother country than because of any actual threat to our country. We have also been in the habit of not daring to ask for what others get as a matter of right, such as the repatriation of our securities, and of disposing of our wheat for less in the hope that gratitude might be our reward. At the time that was a good policy; that was one of the efforts made by the government to ensure those markets after the war; but business is not transacted in that way by Britain. She buys where she thinks she gets the better bargain, be it with yesterday's enemy or tomorrow's potential adversary; and she speaks of imperial loyalty only when she expects it from others.
The moment has come, I submit, to try to impress upon her the advisability of reciprocating in time of peace; this also was suggested this afternoon. We have failed to

The Address-Mr. Brooks
arouse her gratitude; let us try now to convince her that it is in her own best interests to co-operate, that it is in her best interests to trade with us, even if it costs a cent more a pound; and let us provide the dollars she needs by the repatriation operation I have outlined.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to follow closely the arguments we have just heard from the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Picard). I may say, however, that I agree with his statement concerning social security measures for the helpless. I also agree with what he said as to obtaining markets for our farmers. I cannot agree that the farmers of this country are better off than ever before. I know that in my own part of the country the farmers are paying more for what they purchase than they ever paid; and I also know that never in the history of this country was the cost of living as high as it is now.
Neither can I agree with the statement just made by the hon. member for Bellechasse that we should liquidate all our assets in Britain. One great reason Britain was such a great market for our produce in the past was that she had these assets, not only in this country but all over the world, which made it possible for her to purchase goods from all countries. So I cannot agree with the suggestion that we should take away practically everything she has. During the war Great Britain suffered more than any other country; Great Britain helped practically every ally she had, except the United States; and now we should not strip her of her assets and still expect her to be the great market she has been in the past.
Before entering upon a discussion of the matters contained in the speech from the throne I should like to endorse the tributes that have been paid to my late seatmate, Tommy Church. He was deserving of everything that has been said of him. I do not altogether agree that he was old-fashioned in many of his ideas. I believe that the principles he held represented the feelings of more people in this country than we have been led to believe by some of the statements made in this House of Commons.
I want to add my congratulations also, Mr. Speaker, to those extended to the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. They did a good job, there is no question about that. I think they will be quite satisfied with the just praise they have received. I wish to extend my congratulations to the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. (Mr. Picard.]
Harris), who has joined the cabinet ranks. I have congratulated him personally, and all I can say now is that I cannot wish him many long years in the cabinet; but, for the few years in which I expect this government to remain in power, I do wish him every success.
During the debate on the speech from the throne, Mr. Speaker, an opportunity is given hon. members, as representatives of the people, to discuss conditions in the country, and to present to parliament the views of their own constituents concerning the need's of the country as they see them. I shall only touch on a few items this evening, and time will not permit an extensive review of them. I might say that the aftermath of the great war left many problems. One of the greatest problems, of course, was the rehabilitation of our returned men. It also left us with problems in the readjustment of industry, trade, and the whole economy of our nation. These problems extend over a long period1 of years, and a wise government prepares for such problems.
After five years of peace, Mr. Speaker, and after the experience of all countries following the first great war, it was expected that the situation in this country would have been well in hand by now. The readjustment should be complete, but unfortunately this is not the case. We are in the midst of an economic situation which has resulted in the worst unemployment problem we have had since the end of the war. Apparently it is growing worse all the time, despite the assurances we have had from government officials. The debate on the unemployment situation, and on the unemployment insurance bill which was before the house, indicated to this house and to the country the grave situation which faces us.
In my own section of Canada, the maritime provinces, the unemployment figures are the second largest for any part of Canada. This is usually the case in the maritime provinces whenever there is a recession. I was greatly surprised upon reading one sentence in the speech from the throne, to the effect that employment and prosperity remain at a high level in Canada. We all know, Mr. Speaker, that is not a fact. Employment and prosperity do not remain at a high level in Canada. This is particularly true, as I say, in the maritime provinces. We in the maritime provinces are the first to feel a recession because our chief asset is the primary producer. We are not secondary producers. Mining, fishing and agriculture are the industries upon which we depend. It is a well-known fact that any country, or any section of a country, which has to depend on primary products is a section which first feels the depression.

I should like to read a short article from the Moncton Times about the situation in the maritime provinces. It appeared a few weeks ago, and is written by J. P. Crossman. It says:
There is an air of grim foreboding throughout the rural areas of Kent county.
I may say that Kent county is one of the counties in the northern part of New Brunswick.
"There is no work in the woods", is the sad tune, and a brief survey of the situation proves this statement to be a fact.
No more does the ring of the chopper's axe or the whine of the saw pierce the stillness of the forest; gone is the feverish activity which had marked the forest industry of this area in past years. Instead, the farmers, the small woodlot owners and the labourers are idle, awaiting a solution to a problem which is of vital interest to their very existence.
That paragraph, Mr. Speaker, represents the situation in a large area of the maritime provinces.
The article goes on to say:
The forest industry is dead.
That is one of our great industries in the maritime provinces.
A slump in the pulpwood market started the decline early in the year and the loss of the British pit prop market had been the final death blow.
As I said a few moments ago, there is no manufacturing in this section of the country. The people depend upon the forests for a living. For years the long lumber which we shipped to Great Britain was the main industry upon which the people of New Brunswick and part of Nova Scotia depended. That market was lost over a year ago. In past years, hundreds of thousands of cords of pit wood and pulpwood have been shipped overseas and by rail. This has been lost as well. The pit prop industry has meant over $9 million a year to the people of the maritime provinces. When an appeal was made to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Gregg) and to this government to see what could be done about the pit prop industry, the laconic reply was that "pit props were out", and pit props were out, Mr. Speaker. Many of the people in the province of New Brunswick are today unemployed as a result of that.
The people in the northern part of the province of New Brunswick have despaired of any assistance from this government. First, they appealed to the minister from our province. Then they appealed to the local government, but they received no assurance of any action. Today they are taking the matter in their own hands and are sending a delegation to Great Britain to see if they can do what the Minister of Veterans Affairs and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) and the provincial government failed to do for the
The Address-Mr. Brooks people who depend on this industry for a living. It is not only the men in the woods, Mr. Speaker, who suffer as a result of the loss of this trade. There are hundreds of longshoremen in the Miramichi valley, in Richibucto, Chatham and Bathurst, who are also out of work because no pit props or pulpwood have been shipped from the northern part of the province of New Brunswick. In addition to that, the hundreds of men who truck these pit props and pulpwood to the ships are out of employment. The garages have lost business and the merchants have lost business. It is for these reasons that business in the northern part of the province of New Brunswick is practically at a standstill today.
The main reason, Mr. Speaker, for this lack of markets for pit props in Great Britain is the non-convertibility of our currency. For some years, we have pressed for a solution of this problem. If it had not been left to the late date it was, I do not believe we would now be faced with this great problem. A short time ago the Lumbermen's Association met in Montreal, and put forward what they considered might be two solutions for the situation. First, they recommended the lifting of trade restrictions. Second, they said there should be a free exchange of money between countries. I am sure if this could be brought about, Mr. Speaker, it would be of material aid.
I should like to agree with those who have said that the British market is our best market. If that is true for Canada, Mr. Speaker, it is more than true for the people who live in the maritime provinces. For years, we have sold our lumber in Great Britain and in sterling markets of the West Indies. Years ago these were the two great markets for the people of the maritime provinces. Today we have neither of them. We cannot sell to what we call Upper Canada because of the heavy freight rates and the great cost of transportation and also on account of the competition which we have to meet in this market. But if we had the British market and if we had the West Indies market, I believe that the people of the maritime provinces would be prosperous.
I should like to quote none other than a former minister of trade and commerce, Hon. J. A. MacKinnon. Speaking in the city of Saint John a few days ago, when he arrived back from the West Indies, he said:
The people of the British West Indies regret the present trade restrictions with Canada and I heard the proposal advanced that their representatives may approach the Canadian government to see if arrangements can be made whereby this lucrative trade can be expanded.
I hope they do approach our Canadian government, and I hope they come to some

The Address-Mr. Brooks agreement; because I believe it would be of great benefit to the West Indies as well as to ourselves.
I sometimes wonder, Mr. Speaker, if we are buying from Great Britain as much as we could and should. It is a sort of habit for some members of the government to blame Great Britain when we cannot sell certain products to her. But are we buying from her as much as we could? I ask this question after reading an article I saw in Toronto Saturday Night a short time ago, on January 10. It had to do with the purchase of television equipment in this country. Great Britain could have supplied this television equipment; but instead of its being purchased from Great Britain, thus giving us a better opportunity to trade with her, it was purchased from the United States. I think the excuse used was that it was not thought that Great Britain could supply as good material. But as this article says, Great Britain has some of the best technical engineers in the world. She is the country which pioneered in radar. She has also been pioneering in television. Other countries are buying their television equipment from Great Britain. If we want to be [DOT]fair and if we want to get an exchange of currency with which to trade, there is no reason in the world why this large order should not have been given to Great Britain, and there is no reason in the world why the government of this country should not set the example with regard to purchasing from her.

This article goes on to say as follows:
"If Canada won't give us a chance to get into new fields like this," said one British official, "there is no hope whatever of closing the dollar gap-or of our buying more from Canada."
We in certain sections of this country are starving for trade with Great Britain. Our government says that, if Great Britain will sell more goods to us, we shall be able to sell

more goods to her. My point is that when there is an opportunity for us to trade with Great Britain, such as there was in this case, it should have been done if the government is sincere in what it says about developing trade.
I should also like to refer to a similar situation in the United States which also emphasizes the point that I am trying to make. For instance, the city of Seattle in the United States wanted to buy some generators and advertised for tenders. The British put in two bids. The Americans put in certain bids. Great Britain's bids were many thousands of dollars lower than the bids in the United States. What happened? Here is what I read from the Christian Science Monitor:
Here is the story of the first really big effort by the British to act on Washington's advice and take advantage of Washington's formal promise:
The bids were opened, disclosing that there had been seven bidders, of whom two were British, and that the two British bids were very much lower than any of the American bids. Lowest bid was by Ferranti Limited at $515,000. Next lowest was by English Electric at $572,000. Lowest American bid was at $720,000, and other American bids ranged up to $1,321,000.
This was the same company, the General Electric Company; and this article goes on to say that certain excuses were made for not buying from Great Britain. The first one was that the distance from the factory in England to Seattle was too great in case of a breakdown. But as the British pointed out, they had a branch office in Toronto which could have supplied service and attended to any breakdown that might have taken place. They also pointed out that they could have supplied eight generators for the same amount that it would cost to get six generators in the United States.
Then when that excuse did not suffice, it was next said that Ferranti has no experience in building generators for use in such remote and northerly climes. Yet at that very same time Ferranti, that great British company, was building generators for Helsinki in Finland, and had been building this sort of equipment since 1889 and sending it all over the world. The real excuse was given to a reporter by the Seattle purchasing agent who said:
I Imagine we would have had considerable reaction from American manufacturers if we had accepted a British bid.
This article goes on to say:
One of the American manufacturers concerned is General Electric, chairmanned by Philip Reed, who as president of the Anglo-American productivity council is a leading advocate of bigger British sales in the U.S.A.
The British ambassador said: "Do you really want to buy our goods, or don't you?"
I mentioned those two cases, Mr. Speaker, because I think they illustrate that there is

The Address
insincerity somewhere in this country and in the United States with regard to our purchases from Great Britain. As I said a moment ago, in my part of the country at least we feel that every effort should be made to make purchases from Great Britain so that we might be able to sell some of the goods we have, on whose sale depends the very livelihood of the people in that part of the country.
I should like to say a few words with regard to a matter which was before the house the other day, namely, the taking off of trains and the purchasing of coal. It is not necessary for me to deal with this matter to any great extent. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) has already spoken about it, as has the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll), and pointed out that it was not necessary to take off 25 per cent of our trains in the maritimes, and that a million tons of coal could have been obtained by the Canadian National Railways for the service of trains at least in that part of the country. There could also have been coal purchased from these maritime mines for the service of trains in other parts of Canada, had it been looked after at the proper time. The other day the minister said it was only fair, because there was no coal here in Ontario, that all people across Canada should be used alike. That is, because it was not possible to obtain coal for trains here in Ontario we in the maritime provinces, where there is lots of coal, should have our service reduced by 25 per cent.
The city of Saint John and the city of Halifax used to have a midnight train running from Saint John to Halifax, and back from Halifax to Saint John. We had Sunday trains, but these have been taken off. It is hot possible for anyone to travel from either of these two large cities in the maritime provinces from Saturday at noon until Monday at noon.
I do not think such a condition would be accepted' for one moment in any other part of Canada, and in my opinion it would not be inflicted upon any part of Canada except the maritime provinces. I believe it was in 1931 when these trains were taken off once before, and they were off for nearly fifteen years. That was supposed to have been a temporary reduction in our train service. However, they were taken off in 1931 and were not replaced until 1946. I hope the minister will not have the present temporary reduction of service last quite that long.
1 should like to take some time to mention what I believe we need in the maritime provinces. In that part of New Brunswick which has lost its pit prop and pulpwood
-Mr. Brooks business, and where the long-lumber business is out, they need temporary assistance. The government will have to start some public works. But the people down in that section of the country do not want to live on old age pensions, unemployment insurance or mothers' allowances, as they were told by one of the members of the legislature at Fredericton. They want work, and the opportunity to work.
The immediate need, so far as these people are concerned, is a backlog of public works. Towns such as Bathurst, Newcastle, Chatham and others have organized citizens committees, the main object of which is to try to find whatever employment they can for the people living in that section of the country.
Taking the long view of the matter, we want markets for our products. We want the British markets; we want the West Indies market. We also want the development of hydroelectric power in the maritime provinces. In presenting the estimates to the house, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) said, as reported at page 198 of Hansard:
In approving the programs for the various departments' expenditures, the treasury board have had in mind the general economic situation in the maritime provinces and the coastal areas of Quebec, and the government's desire to promote the economic development of this general region, which has encountered greater economic difficulties than the other major regions of the country.
We approve of that statement, and we are wondering just what he is going to do in order to improve the economic position of the maritime provinces. I would tell him what we need. As I said a moment ago, we need markets and, secondly, we need cheap electric power.
I was interested today, as I am sure all hon. members were, to hear about the further development of electric power at Niagara Falls. We have no objection to that, although it will cost many millions of dollars, and will have to be paid in part by those of us from the maritime provinces. We are willing to assist in that project. Then the question was asked: "Will this interfere with the development of the St. Lawrence waterways?" And the answer was "no". There will be power developed along the St. Lawrence river. We in the maritime provinces will help to pay for it, but we will not receive one cent of benefit so far as utilizing that power is concerned.
We have vast quantities of power in the maritime provinces which could be developed, and in justice to those great developments taking place in other parts of Canada, I say

The Address-Mr. Brooks it is only fair that we should receive consideration. As I said before, we want cheap power.
At a recent meeting of the maritime board of trade held in Moncton, New Brunswick, the harnessing of the tides in Passamaquoddy bay was the outstanding matter debated. This is a tremendous scheme, and if undertaken would be one of the largest in that section of the country. It would be a joint undertaking, and has already been investigated by engineers of both the United States and Canada and found feasible.
It is estimated that the development of the tides in Passamaquoddy bay would be capable of producing over half a million horsepower of electricity. This gives some idea of the amount of power that would be available for the development of industry in the province of New Brunswick, as well as in Prince Edward Island and parts of Nova Scotia.
It is believed that the completion of this scheme would witness the beginning of an era that New Brunswick has long looked forward to, and with the cheap power developed that section of the dominion could well be placed on a firm foundation for industrial development. The development of this power has been dreamed of upwards of 40 years.
I repeat, if the government wishes to assist, they should give their blessing to the development of a project such as that.
May I now read from the Toronto Star Weekly of November 19, 1949, regarding this same matter. This article was written by J. E. Belliveau, and states:
"Some day down here in Maine we'll milk our cows by the pull of the moon." That's the prediction of a windbeaten, sturdy old Lubec fisherman. He goes on to say, "and over in New Brunswick," which is so close a bush league pitcher with a fair throwing arm could heave a baseball across the channel and hit Campobello island, "there will be industry unthought of today."
It's not so fantastic as it seems, for strong-minded, down-to-earth easterners long since set out to make reality out of man's ancient dream of harnessing the moon by controlling the tides for electric power. For half a century the idea of trapping the tremendous flow of the Bay of Fundy has been actively considered. One of the world's great hydro engineers, Dexter P. Cooper, started to work out its possibilities as early as 1912. Franklin D. Roosevelt, who was to become president of his country, watched those gigantic tides sweep through the narrow Lubec-Campobello channel in his boyhood. He, too, dreamed dreams and through youth and manhood held on to them. Then, in the 1930's, he went about making them come true.
The Americans started to develop this project in 1930 but, owing to the depression, they abandoned it. But Senator Brewster of the state of Maine, and Senator Smith-I believe the only lady senator in the United States-as well as President Truman, are pressing for it at the present time. We know

that at one time Canada Objected because it was thought it would interfere with our fisheries. I think that has been disproved. Mr. Emery, who was the mayor of Eastport in the United States, a great fish packer, has said that there is nothing in that at all. I think I should like to quote this gentleman who said:
Our economy is seasonal now, both here and in New Brunswick. Quoddy is our only hope. Every engineer consulted says the power can be harnessed. If it is economically reasonable, we know Quoddy will be built, despite all obstacles. We would like to see it settled once and for all. I'm getting on now, been pushing this for 25 years, and it could do me no good. But I would feel satisfied if I could live to see this magnificent scheme become a reality.
There will be other opportunities to discuss this matter. If the government is sincere in wishing to bring economic benefits to the maritime provinces they, if the United States is agreeable, should undertake this project which would help us most of all, a project which could provide cheap power for our provinces.
I hardly think it is necessary for me to mention the Chignecto canal. I do believe that if this project had been proposed in any other part of Canada it would have been carried out long ago. I hope it will receive careful consideration by this government because it will mean much to the people of the maritime provinces. It is not my intention to dwell at length on this tonight except to say that there is not a board of trade, a branch of the Canadian Legion, a Kinsmen's club or a branch of the Knights of Columbus or any other organization in the maritime provinces which is not one hundred per cent behind the development of the Chignecto canal.
In closing may I say I was pleased indeed to note in the speech from the throne that a bill will be introduced to bring veterans of the British and allied forces resident in Canada within the scope of the War Veterans Allowance Act. This is belated justice and should have been done years ago.

Mr. Speaker, my first words shall be to compliment the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne on having been selected by their party for this great honour. The mover, as a young Saskatchewan farmer, in his speech expressed some doubt about the effectiveness of the government's measures to deal with the situation that exists in Canada today. He said, as reported on page 27 of Hansard:
1 feel that I may be open to criticism for not taking issue with the government on some of the matters of a more contentious nature.
I am sure that when he returned to his constituency after the session last year he, along with other Saskatchewan members, was met with criticism of certain actions of the government and expressions of doubt as to the effectiveness of the measures being taken by the government to meet some of the problems facing this country today.
Before dealing further with that however I should like to compliment the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Harris) upon his elevation to the position of Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I am sure he carries the best wishes of members of all groups in the house that he may have success in the organization of that new department and in instituting policies in connection with citizenship and immigration which will be of benefit to the country.
It has always seemed to me that we have neglected citizenship in this country. I can remember when I went to western Canada many years ago. Many of the new people who had come to the country who wanted to get citizenship papers generally applied to a political party. Then just before an election, if the party thought they might secure their support, citizenship papers were obtained for them. As a result many of our new citizens felt a greater allegiance to the political party which had obtained their citizenship papers than they did to the country of their adoption. I think the department should have some educational program for our new citizens. When they secure their citizenship papers the people in the community where they live should have some function or social gathering at which these people would be welcomed as new citizens.
Then a word with regard to immigration. It takes a brave person to say at a time when there are 375,000 unemployed in this country that we should have more immigrants. However, let us look at the situation in Canada.
The Address-Mr. Wright Consider the great iron resources in Labrador and northern Quebec. Consider the great resources of nickel in Sudbury and northern Manitoba. Think of the immense resources of oil in Alberta and Saskatchewan. Yet with all these resources, with the great need we have for development, there are 375,000 unemployed.
Is there any reason for that? Surely there are things to be done in this country which could provide work for the people we have here. What is the situation with respect to our markets? We ship out our resources, in the form of either raw materials or semifinished materials, to Europe to be manufactured into articles which are used here and throughout the world. Then we send food to feed the people who are processing our raw materials.
It seems to me that it would be more sensible if we brought some of those industries to this country, with the people to work in the industries, and processed our raw materials here instead of continuing as we are doing today. We have no markets for our food and yet we are sending our raw materials out of the country to be processed. We are finding ourselves in a position where we cannot get paid for the products that we do ship.
It is a matter of organization, a matter of having a planned economy in the country under which we could not only produce but finish the products from our raw materials. An intelligent immigration policy which would bring industries to this country along with the people to work in them would provide at least a part answer to the problem of markets.
I should like to deal tonight with a matter which I raised the other day in the house at three o'clock. When the report of the Canadian wheat board was tabled I asked if it would be referred to the standing committee on agriculture. Hon. members of the house will recall that in 1947, when the Hon. Mr. MacKinnon was Minister of Trade and Commerce, he told the house that these wheat board reports would be referred to the agricultural committee each year. Unfortunately we have had three years go by without one of them being referred to the committee.

I know that before the last election the government did not give information to the people with regard to quite a few things that were taking place in this country. Among them is the situation which existed as to the wheat board. I hope no one tonight will take anything that I say as criticism of the wheat board or this method of marketing.

Now for a little while I want to deal with the general marketing situation in this country. From the speeches that have been made so far in this debate it is quite evident
The Address-Mr. Wright that there is a serious marketing situation with respect to our agricultural products. I am convinced that we have four major agricultural products for which we must find markets: wheat, cheese, bacon and apples. These four products represent the four main groups of agriculture in this country; wheat in the grain group, cheese in the dairy group, bacon in the meat group and apples in the fruit group. If we can find sufficient markets abroad for our surpluses of these agricultural products we will have a chance within our own economy to balance our production of the other grains, dairy products, meat products and fruits; but we must find markets for those products.
Some say the United States is a market. Well, anyone who has read of the situation that now exists in that country with respect to these products knows there is no market there, that the United States is in a surplus position with respect to each of these commodities. The only long-time market there has been in the past or there is likely to be in the future for these products is the European market, and more particularly the British market. Our failure to sell these products in that market is, in my opinion, largely due to the failure of this government, immediately after the war, to deal with the British government on a bilateral or exchange basis covering our major farm products. If in 1947 this government had been prepared to accept British goods in payment for these products we could have had some of the long-term agreements which have been made with the Scandinavian countries, New Zealand and Australia. At that time we were not prepared to make agreements of that type; as a matter of fact we had no legislation under which that could have been done. We had the acts which had been passed during the war to authorize the sale of these products overseas. Nothing was certain as to the period of time for which that legislation would be constitutional, or for how long it would be carried on. We were renewing it from year to year in this house. Instead of developing a long-term policy dealing with our agricultural products we simply frittered away those markets and only now the results of what we did in 1947 are beginning to be felt. Those markets are gone, and the only way we can hope to get them back is by some arrangement whereby we can accept in payment for our products either British goods or sterling, which can be invested in other parts of the world.
In his remarks during this debate the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) suggested that we should accept sterling for some of our agricultural commodities and

The Address-Mr. Wright invest that sterling in other parts of the world. I was rather surprised to read some of the comments that suggestion drew from various people in responsible positions in Great Britain. I have here the report of a statement by "Adelphi", who, by the way, is Beverley Baxter, Canadian-born Tory member of parliament in Great Britain, who states:
The Times this morning publishes a report that the C.C.F. is urging the Canadian government to accept payment in sterling for a large percentage of its exports to the sterling area. I know that such a suggestion must shake St. James and Bay streets to their foundations, but it is difficult to see how the present rot can be stopped if such a plan is not adopted.
Responsible people in Britain realize that, if they are to buy our products, in some way we must provide them with the dollars or accept their pounds in exchange. Then we can invest those pounds in other parts of the world where such investments can be made to advantage. There are plenty of such places, in the Middle East, in India and in other parts of the sterling area where new developments are needed, and where such developments will help stop the growth and spread of communism. But to insist that we can find markets for those products in the United States is not realistic.
In the speech from the throne it is indicated that we are going to do something with respect to floor price legislation. Hon. members will recall that when the present Agricultural Prices Support Act was introduced in this house in 1944 a great many of us criticized it because it was a temporary measure intended to have effect only during the transitional period. At that time we said this should be permanent legislation, and that the act should contain some formula by which we could determine what were fair floor prices. Neither of our suggestions were accepted. This session, however, we hope to do both those things which should have been done several years ago.
There are two ideas with respect to the method of calculating floor prices for agricultural products. In the United States they have used the term "parity". They have accepted the period from 1909 to 1914, I believe, as the base period, and on that they have established parity floor prices. Under their present plan they pay 90 per cent of parity on some agricultural products such as wheat and cotton; on others they pay 75 per cent and on some perishable products I believe the payment is as low as 60 per cent of parity. In Great Britain and some of the commonwealth countries, as well as Canada, we used a different method to establish floor prices. We used as a basis the long-term contract with Britain. Now, however, as these


contracts cannot be renewed, that method of setting a floor has vanished, and we must find some other method. The minister has suggested that the floor will have to be fairly low.

That was the way the minister's statement was reported in the press. He claims to be misreported so often that it is difficult to know just what he did or did not say, and all I have to go by are the reports appearing in the press. I want to say this, that in establishing floor prices for agricultural products there are two things that must be taken into consideration. These floor prices should be floor prices which are not merely fair to the farmer; they must be established at a sufficiently high level to enable the farmer to maintain the fertility of his soil. Then the farmer can maintain production over a period of years.
If floor prices are established at a low level, merely as a stopgap, it will mean that the farmers will simply mine the soil of this country. That has been done to a great extent for years in this country. It has been done to such an extent in eastern Canada that you can go to the maritime provinces today and find farms that have been abandoned. Go out in the back counties of the province of Ontario and you will see farms that have been abandoned simply because of the low prices for agricultural products. Our soil has been mined to such an extent that it goes out of production. Perhaps that is all right in a country in which you have unlimited soil resources, and where you are opening up new areas. The point has been reached in Canada now where we have not the new areas available. We have reached the point where we have to start building up the agricultural industry of this country on a permanent working basis, on a basis which will maintain the fertility of the soil. Unless we do that, unless we have floor prices which will enable the farmers to farm efficiently and maintain the fertility of the soil, to prevent erosion and to ensure a proper

conservation program for agriculture in this country, we are just building up trouble for ourselves in the future. One of the surest ways we can do this is to set floor prices for our agricultural products so low the farmers will have to continue to mine our soil.
At the last session of parliament, just before the election, the Agricultural Products Marketing Act was passed, under which boards could be set up for the marketing of agricultural products in Canada. I should like to point out, not only to this house but to farm organizations throughout the country, that the farmers themselves have a responsibility in this matter. They cannot expect the government to do something for them which they can do for themselves. The first thing they have to do is to organize their own industry by the setting up of producer boards for the marketing of their particular product. I am however extremely doubtful whether the act that was passed prior to the last election is constitutional, and will give to these boards the power which I believe they will need if they are to be successful.
It seems to me that for any particular agricultural product-let us take hogs for example-if we are to set up boards in this country for marketing, these boards must be set up in each province by the producers in that province. There must be some means, however, by which a central selling agency can be established for the sale of all hogs in Canada. It is not enough to set up a half dozen separate boards with each board having a selling agency, and each agency going out to dispose of that product. If the handling of that product is to be successful, it must all be handled by one board. Not only must it be handled by one board, but that board must keep control of that product until it goes into the wholesale or retail trade of this country. In my opinion, it is not sufficient for the hog producers of this country to set up boards for the sale of their products unless they keep control of that product until it goes into the wholesale or retail trade. It is not enough for them to sell that product to the packers, and then let the packers or cold storage people speculate in that product and make an unfair profit on it.
The Minister of Agriculture himself knows that that is what takes place. When the price of eggs went down last year, he indicated that he was quite displeased with some of the things that had happened in the trade with respect to the marketing of eggs. Last fall, when eggs were bringing approximately 38 cents to the producer, the minister indicated that the consumer was paying 80 cents for the same eggs. Unless these commodity boards set up by the producers keep control of their
The Address-Mr. Wright products and prevent them from falling into the hands of speculators, then I say the boards will not serve the purposes of the producers. As the act reads at the present time, I am rather doubtful whether the boards will have that power. I hope they have, but there is a grave doubt in my mind, and in the minds of many of the agricultural people themselves, as to just how far those boards can go in maintaining control of their product.
It is not good enough to say that these boards should have to take the responsibility for marketing the products when they go outside Canada. I am convinced that we must have export and import boards, controlled by the dominion government, to take control of these surplus agricultural products which must be marketed in the export market. The producer boards have no control over the fiscal policies of this country; they have no control over the tariffs; they have no control over whether dollars will be available for their products when they reach Europe, or the other markets of the world. It is the policies of this government which determine whether those products can be sold when they are exported. This government should take that responsibility, and not throw it back on the producer boards or upon the provinces, as it would appear they are now intending to do.
In this matter of the marketing of agricultural products in the international field, I believe that the government should give serious consideration to backing the food and agricultural organization in its attempt to set up an international commodity clearing house for surplus food products. I was rather surprised to find that the minister, in some of the statements he issued at Washington when this matter was being discussed, indicated he did not believe this commodity clearing house could serve the purpose for which it was intended. On November 25, in the Globe and Mail, the following statement was reported to have been made by the Minister of Agriculture at that conference:
We can see considerable merit, as a long-run development, in the proposal that stocks of food should be held against shortage situations which experience has shown will develop. As has been pointed out in other conferences, however, national governments can, and do, perform this function and we do not see that stocks held by an international agency will, in the short run, contribute to any improvement in the present situation.
The minister has stated here that he believes that is a government responsibility. I hope the government will accept that responsibility and not turn it back on the producer boards or on the province, when it comes to marketing these surplus products in international markets.
