rumours from Nova Scotia are correct, Mr. Speaker, this may be the only opportunity I shall have to address the house before reelection. I therefore wish to place before the government and hon. members of the House of Commons what I understand to be the needs of my constituents in Annapolis-Kings. As one coming from that part of Canada known as the maritimes, of which the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) says "It is practically a different world", I wish to pay my respects and to express my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of the motion.
I am afraid it is only too true that the maritimes are a forgotten, or at least a neglected part of Canada. As a child I was amused by the arguments of the so-called secessionists, or those who would have one believe that they would like to withdraw from confederation and join the United States. As I have become older, and particularly since I have come to Ottawa, I am no longer amused but can see that they were absolutely sincere and had at least some grounds for their complaints.
I do not propose, Mr. Speaker, to go into the matter of maritime rights nor, for that matter, the problems of Nova Scotia as a whole; I propose rather to confine myself as nearly as possible to the grand constituency of Annapolis-Kings which, at the moment, I still have the honour to represent. I think it is a fair statement to make that maritimers, as a whole, know more about Canada than the rest of Canada knows about the maritimes. This is not surprising, because in order for a maritimer to go anywhere he must leave his own section of Canada, and once started, he tends to keep on travelling; whereas the rest of Canada is so large that many residents of Canada outside the maritimes never reach the Atlantic seaboard. I have met many

people in the west who have heard of Halifax and Saint John but who did not have the foggiest idea where Nova Scotia and New Brunswick were.
I have heard many hon. members tell of the richness and of the unlimited resources of their constituencies. I am afraid that I can make no such claims for Annapolis-Kings. As a matter of fact, as far as we know at present, we have no great mineral resources nor have we any great industrial areas. We are entirely a rural section. Even our soil is on the poor side, of a type called podzol, derived from a Russian word meaning ash and indicating a soil highly leached of nutrients and chemicals. Even the so-called fertile Annapolis valley is little more fertile than the rest of the land, except for the marshlands, which are rich alluvial deposits. In that connection I should like to express to the government and to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) our sincere appreciation of the work that has been and is being done under the Maritime Marshland Rehabilitation Act which will add materially to the welfare of our country for future generations. About half the total boundaries of my constituency is water, mainly the bay of Fundy and Minas basin. This is the land made famous by Longfellow's "Evangeline" and by many outstanding men. We are a people steeped in tradition, an old civilization as far as Canada is concerned. Port Royal now Annapolis Royal was settled by the French in 1603; and our whole central valley area was settled for long years before the expulsion of the Acad-dians in 1755. Whatever prosperity we have in our part has been of slow growth and has been built up by generations of industrious, frugal and thrifty people. We have a feeling of permanency, a feeling of always having been there. It is not uncommon to find the fifth and sixth generation on the same farm and the third and fourth generation in the same house.
We in Nova Scotia are a long way from the markets of central and western Canada, and are traditionally a seafaring race-and especially was that so in the day of iron men and wooden ships-so that the natural market for our products is Great Britain, the New England states, Cuba and the British West Indies.
Before going more fully into this phase of our economy I should like to draw to the attention of the government and hon. members one or two matters of some importance to us. The proposal to extend the coverage of the Unemployment Insurance Act to employment in hospitals and charitable institutions has raised a storm of protest in our part of the country and all through the 55946-19
The Address-Mr. Elderkin maritimes. As an example, I might cite the case of the Eastern Kings Memorial hospital in Wolfville, of which little hospital we are very proud. The only reason I choose the Wolfville hospital as an example rather than any of the four other excellent hospitals in Annapolis-Kings is that, as a member of the board of trustees for a number of years, I am very familiar with conditions there. It is a hospital of only thirty-bed capacity, but for a good many years it has been approved by the American College of Surgeons. In this hospital we have an efficient staff of nurses and doctors. Contrary to the experiences of many of the larger hospitals, we have little difficulty in keeping a fine group of nurses. This is largely on account of the "happy family" attitude which prevails among the doctors, nurses and others of the staff. In spite of this harmonious and efficient operation, we had a small deficit in 1948 but in 1949, even after an increase in rates, our deficit was nearly $7,000. I should like to urge the government to consider the matter carefully before they do anything which would increase costs to our hospitals already staggering under a heavy load.
In Kings county we have had for many years at Aldershot a military camp which has been used very little for training purposes since the end of world war II. I should like respectfully to suggest to the Minister of National Defence (Mr, Claxton) that Aider-shot camp be used as much as possible as a peacetime training camp.
Lest I might be considered unduly critical I should like to commend the Minister of National Defence and the government for reopening H.M.C.S. Cornwallis and the R.C.A.F. station at Greenwood. Much as we deplore the necessity of spending so much on defence, I believe all hon. members on both sides of the house agree that these expenditures cannot be avoided.
We have in Annapolis-Kings a good many fishermen who have their special problems of production, processing and marketing. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, I should like to explain some of the peculiarities of the fishing grounds from which our fishermen try to wrest a living. Almost the whole coast of my constituency is rugged and rocky, with these rocky shores washed by the tides and storms of the bay of Fundy and Minas basin.
The bay of Fundy, as some hon. members may know, is noted for its extremely high tides-a rise and fall occurs daily from 20 feet to an extreme high of 60 feet or more. For anyone who has no experience with these high tides and consequently with the tremendous currents of this region, it is almost
280	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Elderkin impossible to realize conditions as they are. Even a moderate wind will kick up a very high sea, if tide and wind are opposed. Off Blomidon the rush and roar of the waters a\ certain times of the tide are almost unbelievable, and although not so spectacular as Niagara, the water that flows over Niagara would be a mere trickle compared with what flows by cape Split four times each twenty-four hours. With these strong currents our fishermen have at all times to contend and they must adapt themselves to the tides and in fact use them to their own advantage.
On this particular coast we have no low-water harbours and boats must enter and leave at half-tide and in many cases at three-quarter tide. This often means that in times of sudden storm they may not be able to run for shelter but have to ride it out until such time as the tide is right. In the case of a bad nor'easter they may not be able to make harbour at all; consequently during the stormy seasons our fishermen are very careful about going out to the fishing grounds for fear that they cannot get in and may be storm-stayed out in the dangerous bay of Fundy.
This makes their fishing season shorter than it might be if there were deep-water harbours. Therefore, anything that may reduce their catch at any time seriously affects their livelihood, and hence their objection to draggers, which they claim not only deplete the supply of haddock and cod but also disturb the feeding grounds so that it is almost hopeless to catch the fish remaining after the draggers are through.
To explain this a little, the fishing grounds of the bay of Fundy are not made up of a continuous shelf or bank. The floor of the bay of Fundy is much like the shore line with hills and hollows, ups and downs, with the feeding grounds generally on the peaks or higher ridges.
When the draggers get through with these ridges the tides take over and move the disturbed feed. It has not yet been determined whether these feeding grounds are merely moved or if they are temporarily destroyed, but it has been definitely determined that some time elapses before feed is again available there.
The fishing section of my constituency extends from Victoria Beach on the extreme west and Delaps Cove in the northwest to Scotts Bay at the easterly end, a distance of roughly 130 miles. The westerly half of this shore line is along that part of the bay of Fundy which could most rightly be called a part of the Atlantic ocean, but the farther east we go the narrower the bay of Fundy becomes, and as the bay becomes narrower, so the 

objections to the activities of the draggers become greater, as it is here they interfere most with the "inshore" fishermen.
Our Canadian draggers are supposed to keep outside the 12-mile limit but the American draggers may legally come to the 3-mile limit. I do not know that any American draggers have been in this area to which I have reference, but Canadian draggers certainly have been and are quite careless about distance, especially after dark.
Besides the conventional draggers we now have smaller vessels 40 feet long, or shorter, and these smaller ships do not comply with any 12-mile limit nor with the 3-mile limit but may, and often do, come close inshore, dragging lobster traps, herring nets, weirs and trawls.
I should like to urge the government through the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. May-hew) thoroughly to investigate the fisheries and fishing conditions of the bay of Fundy area in an endeavour to discover the best solution of their problems so that the fishermen of my section may take their proper place in the economy of our great nation.
I should like to go on record as being in favour of a complete and independent survey of the Chignecto canal.
It is thought by many people, even in Nova Scotia, that we in Annapolis-Kings produce apples and little else. This is far from true, for Kings county alone even before world war II produced agricultural products, other than apples, to a value greater than any other county in Nova Scotia.
We had at one time a very lucrative trade with Cuba and the British West Indies, mostly in potatoes and fish. These have now been almost entirely lost with the exception of the sale of certified seed potatoes. Various nefarious jugglings were responsible for the loss of these markets. Perhaps the one most responsible for this loss was "Sugar Daddy" Rhodes, who, while minister of finance under a Conservative regime, put increased duties on sugar. I would ask hon. members opposite if it is any wonder Annapolis-Kings goes Liberal most of the time. After the loss of these markets for fish and potatoes our fishermen became poverty stricken, and our potato growers either quit growing potatoes or went bankrupt.
Shut out by tariff walls from the markets to which we had cheap and ready access by water freight, we became more dependent upon our sales of apples to Britain, which country, up to the outbreak of war in 1939, was a free open market in which we found ready sale for nearly all we could produce.

During the war we were, generally speaking, able to find a ready market for any farm product we produced with the exception of apples, which was a war casualty, and about which I propose to speak later.
I should like here to quote a few figures to show the increase in production of some of our agricultural products during the past few years. Poultry increased in numbers from 300,000 in 1941 to 800,000 in June, 1949; hogs from 13,000 in 1941 to 19,000 last year. Dairy production increased 10 per cent in the last five years. Potato acreage increased 20 per cent since 1941. Pears increased from 300 acres in 1939 to 700 acres in 1949. Plums have increased about 18 per cent in the past 10 years, while small fruits and vegetables have increased 50 per cent.
You can see from this brief summary, Mr. Speaker, that we have been trying to diversify our farm economy. For the first few years after the war we were able to sell our increased production at reasonable prices, but now we find ourselves in about the same position in regard to markets as we were before the war, although local purchasing power is much better than in 1939, and we also have a somewhat increased consumer population.
We farmers have been told and are being told that we should not put all our eggs in one basket but should diversify. This we are quite willing to do and capable of doing if we only have a market for our products.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, even before the war the rail-haul to the markets of central Canada was too expensive for most of our products; but now, with our freight rates increased from 30 per cent to 50 per cent over former rates, central Canada is just that much farther away.
We are also handicapped in my part of the country by the fact that our season for strawberries, plums, cherries, and all early vegetables is somewhat later than in central Canada, so that at the time our early tomatoes and other early vegetables and fruits are ready for market we find carloads of Ontario produce being dumped in Nova Scotia. It takes only a few carloads of Ontario fruits or vegetables to glut our home market. By the time we are at peak production our market is saturated with supplies from outside Nova Scotia.
Then let us take a look at a product like carrots, which we can grow readily and economically in many parts of my constituency, but for part of which we must find a market outside Nova Scotia. According to government statistics, on February 1 of this year there were in the whole of Canada 8,196 tons of carrots in storage. Of this amount 1,787 55946-192
The Address-Mr. Elderkin tons were in Nova Scotia. With the price in Montreal being only about 2 cents a pound for domestic grown carrots, owing to the new crop coming in from the United States, what chance have we of clearing up the balance of last year's crop, or what incentive is there to plant a new crop?
Another crop which is normally salable in
Canada with little difficulty is cranberries. It costs anywhere from $1,000 to $2,500 per acre to put a cranberry bog in proper condition to produce berries. The sprinkler system alone costs $1,500 per acre. Cranberries take several years before they come into production, but with proper care and frost protection will give satisfactory yields of good quality berries for many years.
Normally Canada does not raise sufficient cranberries for her own use and until fairly recent years the volume and quality was so uncertain that a proper demand could not be built up; but now with improved methods and more knowledge both the quality and supply are reasonably adequate.
Cranberries, like many other products, come under the Geneva and Annecy agreements and consequently there does not appear to be any way to impose quotas or restrictions on Cape Cod berries coming into Canada until tariffs come up for revision this year.
In 1948, owing to the imposition of exchange
regulations, no cranberries came from Cape Cod into Canada, and as the Canadian supply was limited the prices went very high, the wholesale price in Montreal in November of that year being $9.90 for a 25-pound box, and in December it rose to $11.13 per box.
With the lifting of exchange restrictions in 1949 Cape Cod berries came in a regular flood, a total of 3,725,000 pounds entering Canada last year. Of course, prices dropped until in November, 1949, the wholesale price in Montreal of Canadian-grown cranberries was $2.62 per box; in December the price rose to $2.99. What hopes for cranberries?
If our products are shipped C.P.R. to Montreal they must be handled and rehandled because of the lack of a car ferry between Saint John and Digby. If these products are shipped D.A.R. and C.N.R. to Montreal, they not only have an extra long haul but travel over two rail systems.
As we are all aware, it is impossible to build up and hold a market for perishable farm products without cheap and adequate transportation; as transportation improves so does the prosperity of the country.
In this connection I should like with your permission to quote in part from an announce ment made in this house on December 7,

The Address-Mr. Elderkin 1949, with regard to steamship service by the Minister of Transport, as reported on page 2829 of Hansard. He said:
At the present time the S.S. Yarmouth operates between Yarmouth and Boston during the summer months, making three trips per week.
And again:
It is felt that if this vessel is going to discontinue the service, some method should be found to increase the number of tourist cars which may be carried to Nova Scotia during the summer season. Both governments likewise feel that the situation cannot be left in a state of uncertainty, and that the tourist traffic into Nova Scotia should not only be maintained but increased.
I am therefore pleased to announce that it has been decided to build a vessel which will not only be adequate to carry the present traffic but which will serve to increase the tourist trade between Nova Scotia and the United States. The proposed vessel will be a fast modern car ferry with a capacity of about 200 cars and about 1,000 passengers. The service will be based on Yarmouth, and will operate between that port and a port in the eastern United States. Being a modem vessel it will offer facilities considerably better than those now available, at a much cheaper cost to tourists and more in line with present and anticipated needs.
With this I am quite in accord but I would suggest that this announcement does not go far enough. We in Annapolis-Kings will welcome any increase in tourists resulting from this move, for we like their money and with possible exceptions we like them for themselves. Moreover, we like people to enjoy the beauty of our very beautiful country.
I would respectfully say to the government that I do not believe our tourist business in itself will go very far in solving the economic problems of our section of Nova Scotia, and I would further suggest that in the planning of the ship, serious consideration should be given to its adaptability for fast, efficient and economical freight. If we had efficient, economical and dependable freight service from Yarmouth to a port in the eastern states near a good market with the ship arriving at the United States port at the proper time of day, the economic problems of western Nova Scotia would be half solved. If, in addition to this efficient water service, we had a reduction in the tariff on our primary products entering the United States, I believe we could solve our own problems as far as small fruits and vegetables are concerned.
If something of this kind could be worked out it would be only a few years until we would be producing large quantities of small fruits and vegetables, strawberries, blueberries, both wild and cultivated, raspberries, plums, and believe it or not, cherries. The lower part of Annapolis county is a natural for the production of cherries. Besides these

products we would have an extended market for poultry and poultry products, choice beef, veal and dairy products.
Our fishermen would benefit also from this outlet and could land fresh and frozen fish, lobsters and scallops in the Boston market. Give us a fast, efficient, economical water freight service, with reduced tariffs, and we will do the rest. I do not think that this is too much for us, from that place which is "practically a different world", to ask of a Liberal government, which does not need the name "progressive" tacked onto it to be really progressive.
I should like to speak for a few minutes about our apple problem. I should say at the outset that I know the problem but that I have no ready solution unless we can within a few years regain at least a part of our old market in Britain. I should like, if I have time, to briefly sketch the growth of the Nova Scotia apple industry up to 1939, present the problem as it then appeared, tell what we as growers have tried to do to remedy the situation, what assistance we have had from the Canadian government and what we should like the government to do for us now.
The first recorded plantings of apples in the Annapolis valley was in the early seventeenth century at Port Royal. Apples did not take on any great commercial significance until after 1850, when occasional shipments were made to England in small sailing vessels. But as transportation facilities became better our plantings of apple trees became greater. These plantings were largely of varieties which at that time were acceptable to the British consumers and consisted largely of culinary or cooking varieties to which our soil and climate seemed particularly well adapted. Our production continued to increase with the emphasis in a large degree on volume and economy of production as the consumers of our fruit were mostly people of very moderate or low income.
We always had insect pests in our Nova Scotia orchards but until after 1900 they were of major importance only at periodic intervals. In addition to insect pests we have always had apple scab, or black spot, as it is often called. This scab is a cool-weather fungus and appears to grow best in cool wet weather, of which we have a great deal in Nova Scotia.
It was not until after the first world war that -we began to spray in earnest and it took some years for us to find that we could grow varieties like McIntosh which are very susceptible to scab. In fact, as late as 1924 the experimental station at Kentville advised

The Address-Mr. Elderkin
against the planting of McIntosh and similar varieties as they were not deemed suitable for our climate. Moreover, we were catering almost entirely to the British market where even for dessert purposes the taste appears to be different from that on this side of the Atlantic. In Canada the demand was largely for large red apples of somewhat softer texture and by and large sub-acid. In Britain, however, they wanted a crisper, chewier, more acid apple or as they often said, "apples with character". The three most popular dessert varieties which we grew for the British trade were Cox Orange, Golden Russet and Ribston Pippin, none of which can we sell in volume in Canada at anywhere near production costs. It is true that there was a place for large red apples on the English market but they were largely like the King, a dual purpose apple, an excellent cooker but also of good eating quality. Most of our export varieties were of green, yellow or a russet colour.
This was partly because the English growers grew these kinds and the public was accustomed to them and also partly because our climate is such in most years that we can grow that type more economically than the red varieties which require more sunshine and care. During the 1920's we had almost continuous bad growing years. The 1930's were generally speaking good apples years in spite of bad winter injury in 1933-34, of severe frosts in 1936 and two disastrous gales, each from different directions, in 1937. In spite of these handicaps we produced an average yearly crop of almost six million bushels for the years 1936-38. In 1939 we had a crop of slightly over six million bushels.
It was apparent even during the thirties that we must not rely too heavily on the British market as their production was increasing so that in years when they had big crops most of our apples were not wanted and sold for low prices.
Up to 1912, when the United Fruit Company of Nova Scotia was formed, most growers packed and shipped their own fruit or sold to dealers, first largely tree run but later mostly on a packed-out basis. With the advent of co-operative companies there was a decline in grower packing and also in selling to apple dealers. In Nova Scotia a grower had four choices: he could sell on the local market, could himself ship to England, sell to dealers, or market co-operatively. Let us again note that the emphasis was on quantity not quality, economy not excellence During the years the Nova Scotia fruit growers were constantly striving to get varieties which were more productive and more
profitable, but a great many were of little or no value and were only removed by death or grafting. Others like McIntosh, Cortland and Delicious were valuable but they all added to the numbers so that in 1939 we had nearly 200 different varieties.
We packed almost entirely in barrels, which was a strong, cheap package capable of easy and rapid handling. Some boxes were packed as early as 1910 and some progressive growers were forever trying different types of package. In nearly all cases the grower returned to barrels as netting him the most profit. I have seen in the past few years so-called new packages which were almost identical with those we had tried and found1 unprofitable.
Thus when war broke out in 1939 we found ourselves with a crop of over two million barrels composed mostly of varieties not readily salable in Canada under any condition and owing to the war our overseas market was almost entirely lost. If we had attempted to market this crop in Canada it would have been ruinous not only to us but also to the other apple-producing areas in Canada. After discussions with the federal government it was decided that something should be done. As a result of this the Nova Scotia apple marketing board was set up through which all Nova Scotia apples produced in the commercial apple areas of Nova Scotia must be marketed. In fact, what the government did was to buy up all the Nova Scotia apples which could not be sold on the fresh fruit markets and process them. Of the 1939 crop half a million barrels were sold as fresh fruit overseas and on the domestic market, and over one and a half million barrels were processed. In that way the Canadian market was largely left for Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia. This type of assistance has been rendered to the Nova Scotia apple industry every year up to 1949, except that the form of assistance varied somewhat from year to year. The endeavour was to process enough Nova Scotia apples so that our fruit wbuld not interfere too much with that grown in the rest of Canada.
This scheme really was remarkably successful, as anyone familiar with the apple picture in Canada knows. The last six or seven years have been the most prosperous for the apple growers of Canada of any similar period, with the exception of Nova Scotia growers. Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia growers have never known such prosperity.
What then of Nova Scotia with all the millions of taxpayers' money that was poured into our industry? It is quite true that 1946 was a banner year with over two million barrels of good apples. There was a large
2S4

The Address-Mr. Elderkin sale to Britain at excellent prices and our growers did make a profit. But for all the other years from 1939 to 1949 most growers lost money on their apples. If you accept that statement I must answer two or three questions. First, where did the money go? It went partly to the growers for production costs but largely to pay for processing that portion of the crop that was taken off the fresh fruit market. Perhaps you will say too much went in profit on fertilizers and spray materials. As to that, the margin of profit was fixed by the wartime prices and trade board, and for the past five or six years most of these supplies were furnished by co-operative fruit companies so that whatever profit was left went back to the growers in any event.
How then did they live and thrive if they lost money on their apples? That is the easiest question of all to answer. Up to 1949, and even for part of that year, we could sell at a profit, apart from some exceptions which always occur with farm products, practically everything we produced, beef, hogs, eggs, poultry, milk, plums, pears, potatoes, small fruits and vegetables. Why then were Nova Scotia orchardists so unwise as to continue producing at a loss? Nothing but blind faith in Britain, that she would soon be able to buy our apples again, and the knowledge that we could produce at least as cheaply as any other section. What have we been doing for ourselves? First we have made a concentrated effort to convert our orchards to highly coloured dessert varieties more readily salable in Canada. This has been done largely by new plantings and by grafting. In 1948 alone over 40,000 trees were grafted.
We have removed over 700,000 trees that were either old or of undesirable varieties. We have erected four large modem cold storage plants where boxes and other small packages are stored, packaged and shipped, and all other warehouses are now equipped to pack in packages smaller than barrels. We have had one desk selling for the past eleven years.
The fact remains that there are more apples produced in Canada than can be sold here, and in the meantime we in Nova Scotia are still producing too many varieties which have little sales appeal on local markets and not yet enough of the desirable varieties, for it takes years to change over apple orchards. It cannot be done in two or three years. Even though we have already destroyed over
700,000	ti'ees, I believe we should remove at least an additional 300,000 this year.
I should like to trace briefly tree removal in Nova Scotia from 1939 to date. In 1939 some of us rented heavy tractors from the
(Mr. Elderkin.)
provincial government and removed old and/ or undesirable varieties. No record was kept of the numbers removed that year. In 1940 and 1941 the Nova Scotia government provided tractors free for tree removal. About
100.000	trees were removed in these years. As it is quite expensive to remove tree debris and rehabilitate the land, and as farmers were hard up, the federal government was asked for assistance. From 1943 to 1946, 231,477 trees were destroyed under a bonus of $2 per tree. Trees destroyed had to be from commercial orchards and able to meet requirements as to size and bearing capacity. The Nova Scotia government supplied free tractors for this work.
There was no tree removal policy in 1947. But when it was realized that we would not likely have an open market in Great Britain for some years, an arrangement was entered into with the federal government in 1948 for assistance in the removal of an additional
300.000	trees. We were in this case attempting with government assistance to eliminate good commercial trees of varieties formerly acceptable in Great Britain.
I wish to take this opportunity of expressing the sincere thanks of our growers for all that the government of Canada has done through the years to save this valuable industry. I realize that our growers would also wish me to express thanks for the assistance and co-operation rendered by the government of my province. In conclusion, I would not be doing my duty if I did not impress on the government and hon. members of the house the necessity of making good the loss suffered in the marketing of last year's crop. Until the rehabilitation of our fruit growers is completed, it would seem that the apple growers of Nova Scotia require a government assistance program for that portion of our crop which cannot be sold on the fresh fruit market. In addition to the
700.000	trees that have already been destroyed, it is absolutely necessary to have public assistance that will ensure the removal of another 300,000 trees this year.

and hon. gentlemen-

speechtext:
I heard somebody remark that it is out of order to say "hon. gentlemen", and if so I am sorry. I believe it is customary to compliment the mover (Mr. Larson) and the seconder (Mr. Dumas) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. In this particular instance I am more than pleased inasmuch as the hon. member for Kindersley (Mr. Larson) is a fellow colleague

from the province of Saskatchewan. He discharged his duty in a most creditable manner. I am sure all hon. members of the house will join with me in extending to him the highest compliments. The same remarks apply to the seconder.
The qualifications I have as the member for the constituency of Qu'Appelle are those of a woman beater. I do not want that remark to be construed in such a way that the female sex will be prejudiced against me. Frankly, I have a great deal of respect and regard for them, but nevertheless I am here as a woman beater. Turning now to the constituency of Qu'Appelle, at this time I should like to mention a former member, the late Ernest Perley who, while of a different party, was a personal friend of mine. Politically we were opposed, but as personal friends we were very close. Then of course there is the very good lady whom it was my pleasure to defeat in the last election.
The riding of Qu'Appelle is essentially a rural one. It is one of the wealthiest and one of the best ridings in the Dominion of Canada, if not the best. The wealth of the Qu'Appelle riding stems from agricultural products, and by virtue of that quite naturally I am interested in seeing that their agricultural products will be sold at prices which will permit the people whom I represent to carry on their farming operations on a basis that will provide them with a good income and a good standard of living. I stand for the retention of the Crowsnest pass freight rates, as I think every hon. member from western Canada should; and I hope no one anywhere in Canada will ever undertake to alter those rates.
Then we have the wheat board. For the major portion of my business life I was in the grain trade, and during that period I was opposed to compulsory marketing and such things as the wheat board and the wheat pools. However, in later years I had the opportunity of studying some of the hardships which were caused by the rise and fall of wheat prices, and as a result I have come to firmly believe in the principle of wheat board marketing. I stand for that and will fight for it; and I know those whom I represent in the riding of Qu'Appelle will want me to make this statement.
I believe the marketing of coarse grains is being handled in the only sensible way. That is a commodity which for the most part is consumed within our own boundaries. When it is remembered that approximately eighty per cent of our coarse grains are marketed within Canada it will be seen that the board is placed in a rather difficult position when it is exDected to be both buyer and seller.
The Address-Mr. Dewar Naturally we in the west are on the tail of the wheat board to get the price up; naturally those in the east and in the feeder markets are on the tail of the board to keep prices down.
We have the P. F. A. A., which in my opinion is one of the finest act's ever passed by the House of Commons. The principle is good, and as far as 1 can see the method is the best that has been devised to date. I do not say something better may not be discovered, but it is the best we have found so far. The only suggestion I would make in passing is that I believe the time is long past when the governments of Saskatchewan and Alberta should also recognize their responsibilities. Unfortunately there is altogether too much of this wanting provincial autonomy and then, when it is offered, saying, "No, it is a federal responsibility". So I suggest that in the borderline or isolated cases the provincial governments should begin to assume some of the responsibility that is rightfully theirs.
I have a note here under the heading "water", and you will notice that I just had a drink. It is a very important commodity. We have the P. F. R. A., which deals with water conservation and the construction of small dugouts for farmers. Those who have not had the privilege, which I have had, of seeing what these have meant to the farmers in western Canada cannot fully appreciate the importance of these projects. The work has been well done; the money devoted to the development of these small dugouts on the farms has been wisely spent. When you see the little orchards, the little groves of trees, the water systems on the farms, the pressure systems in the houses, you realize that this is a wonderful thing.
Then in Alberta we have the irrigation projects. Those hon. members coming from that province who have seen irrigation systems in action and have seen their advantages will appreciate the value of those great works. In the Fraser valley we have the diking-

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Snow banks.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, snow banks. They mean water, and water often means trouble. They have had a lot of trouble in the Fraser valley, and I am afraid they are going to have a lot more. The diking program which has been embarked upon by this government is going to mean a great deal to the people of the Fraser valley. In the eastern part of our country we have the marshland reclamation project. That is also a wonderful thing.
All these matters deal with water. In our own province we have the South Saskatchewan river project. I think I should note in passing that of all hon. members of this house I am the onlv one who has lived within a

The Address-Mr. Dewar ' short distance of the proposed site of the South Saskatchewan river development dam. I lived there for a number of years, so I think I can speak authoritatively as to the problem, as to the need and as to the urgency of developing this project. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has suggested both last session and this session that the minister representing Saskatchewan and the government of that province should hang their heads in shame, but I say that is not so. You just do not embark upon a scheme involving the expenditure of fifty, a hundred or a hundred and fifty million dollars without investigating the potentialities. After all is said and done Canada is a nation; it is not just a matter of one isolated spot. Therefore when I say this is a proper expenditure to be made, I have in mind the need for the project and the urgency in relation to it. Some time ago in the Regina Leader-Post there appeared an article headed "River betrayal plan" by the attorney general of that province, a chap by the name of Corman. He says we have betrayed the people, and that we are going to compel the Saskatchewan government to pay half the cost of approximately $100 million or the dam will not be proceeded with. That statement is absolutely wrong; that was never said. We want to make sure that the provinces where we are spending money on water conservation make use of that water. There is no point in building a dam on the South Saskatchewan if the water is just going to lie there for a few fish to swim in or for someone to take a bath now and again. That water must be utilized.
Then on this continent we have the St. Lawrence waterway development scheme, which has been under discussion for a good many years. If people will just stop and look at the geographical set-up of this country they will see that we have the greatest inland water system of any nation in the world, and it is at our very doorstep. Let us not lose sight of that fact. Everything we have has to do with water. I hear an hon. member say I am full of water. Well, I would hate to say what he is full of. Today we are living in the greatest paradox imaginable in connection with this commodity called water. In Ottawa we are at the junction of two rivers, but we find that in the summertime there is not enough water available to permit people to water their lawns. If you go to Montreal you find the same situation. They have the same problem in Vancouver; yet they are living adjacent to water everywhere. If eight weeks ago I had made the statement that water was one of the most essential and most critical things we have in Canada I might have been laughed at, and possibly I will be 
laughed at now. Had I forecast eight or ten weeks ago that a city the size of New York would be brought to its knees due to a shortage of water somebody might have said, "Oh, bosh; he doesn't know what he is talking about." Today, New York cannot expand. It is all right for you to laugh, my friend, if you wish, but water is one of the most important commodities we have in Canada. If you have not got water, if it is not conserved and properly utilized, continued existence is not possible.
The point I am trying to make, Mr. Speaker, is this. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) is the one man in Canada who has taken a concrete, forward step with regard to this matter. He has fought inch by inch for these water developments. He has had the foresight to do so. I am wondering whether we in this parliament today, whether we of this generation in the Dominion of Canada, are going to have the foresight necessary to make provisions for the development of the water resources of this country. We talk about the Hudson Bay railway, and I am in favour of it. I am in favour of utilizing every facility we have in the Dominion of Canada. We think this railway is a great thing, but it is only a bagatelle in comparison with the development of the St. Lawrence. At least 4 cents per bushel will accrue to the western farmer on every bushel of wheat that is sold, to say nothing of the inland development which will take place.
Today there was an announcement with respect to power. There is a great paradox again, power. We have gone to bed on it, but not the dominion government. Consider the potential power in the St. Lawrence, 2,200,000 horsepower. It is sitting there at our back door. I have been in Ottawa for six or eight months, and about a month ago was about the first time I ever saw all the lights turned on. I tell you it is time we got down to a bit of realistic thinking. Some people say it is the fault of the federal government, but it is not. If one looks at all the documents and follows the correspondence through, examines the research that has been done since the plan originated back in 1938, one finds that the blame can be put on the congress of the United States. Probably I should not say that, but it is not a government statement, it is my statement. For the purpose of keeping the New York state vote, congress has not touched the St. Lawrence development. In the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and the adjacent states in the United States, we have everything at our doorstep short of power, it is for that reason I suggest that the time is long past when we in the Dominion of Canada should recognize our responsibilities,

and not be concerned with today or tomorrow, but think in terms of ten years from now. We should develop our water resources.
I am going to turn to the question of trade now, and more specifically to the question of trade with Great Britain. We have heard many references to British trade today. At this time I should like to say that I agree with the remarks the Minister of Agriculture made in this house last fall. I believe he has repeated this statement since then, but he suggested there seemed to be an organized attempt on the part of British officials to do away with trade agreements. Having said that, I expect some comments will be made upon it. I am not saying that the British people do not want to trade with us. They not only want to trade with us, but they want and need our products. During our peak period of trade in agricultural products in L94U or 1947, it amounted to approximately $450 million. Today, hon. members have said our trade has fallen apart. If they will check the figures, I believe they will find that last year we did approximately $400 million worth of business with the United Kingdom, which is only approximately $50 million less than the all-time high. I do not think this government should hang its head in shame over a record like that.
Further than that if our position today is reviewed, I fully believe the contracts we now have, and the business that will be done with the United Kingdom in the ensuing year, will come close to that figure. I believe all of us in this house appreciate, not necessarily fully understand, some of the suffering and hardship through which the people of Great Britain have passed during those trying years of war and since that time. Great Britain has had a lot of help from Canada. Possibly the trade agreements that were made were made with the understanding that after the war Canada would get a better deal. Apparently, that is not so. I should like to say now that I am rather surprised that the minister in charge of these contracts in Great Britain, or in charge of the purse strings, would do what he did when it came to a matter of making the odd contract for our eggs, cheese and a few such small items. For the sum of approximately $30 million, the British government has engendered the ill will of the producers of eggs, milk and cheese in Canada.
I believe the responsibility for this lies at the door of the ministry in Great Britain. It is my understanding that Great Britain has undertaken to have on hand when Marshall plan aid ends in 1952 the sum of $2 billion in dollar reserves. A few years ago Great Britain started to accumulate this sum. Today she has approximately $1,860 million of that
The Address-Mr. Dewar reserve, and there is still about two years to run. If anyone in this house can tell me where the common sense lies in engendering the ill will of the producers of this country for the sake of $30 million, as against $2 billion, when she already has $1,860 million, I should like to be shown. I cannot reconcile it, myself. If that is the type of government Great Britain has, I fear for the future of Great Britain.
I note that in a speech that was delivered by the member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming), a part of which appears at page 140 of Hansard, he said:
Figures from the dominion bureau of statistics show that the value of our field crops alone in Canada in 1949 fell by 16 per cent as compared with 1948, from a total of 31,696 million in 1948 to $1,427 in 1949.
Why did the hon. member not tell the rest of the story? It reminds me of the great Disraeli; you all know Disraeli. During the course of a debate in the House of Commons he is said to have remarked that there are lies, damned lies and statistics. These happen to be statistics which the hon. member is using, but he is using them to misrepresent the facts. The hon. member will point a finger over here and say that we have done this, but you have done that. But it is all right if he gets up and misinterprets. Did he tell you the rest of the story? He mentioned 16 per cent. Did he tell you that practically half of the province of Saskatchewan, the biggest agricultural value-producing area in the Dominion of Canada had no crop and had nothing this year? Does that not more than account for the 16 per cent? He did not tell you that, did he? I am telling you. I want to correct that impression. Then he goes on a little further on and says:
Under the control system they sacrificed more than $500 million as a result of the government's wheat policy alone. Our farmers were not permitted to sell their wheat on the free markets of the world. Today those same farmers are being deprived of the promised fruits of that policy.
The first comment I am going to make is this. This afternoon the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) stated that the farmers had lost one billion dollars. About a week ago the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) said that they had lost a half a billion dollars. Just about ten days ago or less the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) stated that the loss had been two billion dollars. If they are going to state that the farmers have lost something, I wish to heaven they would get together on the amount; then, having got together on the amount which the farmers lost, they might submit some proposal to the government and the government might act on it. But I suggest that no loss was incurred, and I want to tell you the story.

At the time the war started, I was in the grain business, on the line. Under the Canada Grain Act, the grain companies must buy all the grain that is offered. But the war came. There was no chance for these dealers or grain companies to sell their grain. So what did they do? They came pit pat, pit pat to the Canadian government and said, "Will you help us out?" If the grain exchange had stayed open, the farmer would not have obtained anything for his grain, because they could not sell it. That is the first thing.

We were fighting a war and the money that was going towards the buying of that wheat came from where? It came out of the credits that this government established in this country on a lend-lease basis for Great Britain; in other words, it came out of the pockets of the taxpayers. So we could have put the price up to $2 a bushel, but it would not have meant anything. But we said, "No; we are going to hold the line", and we did it most successfully. If the government did nothing else during the war years, it held down inflation; and I am proud to be associated with men who had the foresight to do that. Having said that, I will proceed.
The grain exchange were quite happy to take their profits on storage. They had no chance of losing any money. They took their storage charges. They were able to write off those balloon-type bins they built and charge it up against profits. But as soon as the war ended, when even a Chinaman could have sold wheat to anybody, what did they do? They came to the government and said, "Give us back the wheat. We want to sell it". Do you suppose for one minute that the producer would have shared in those profits?

Motion agreed to and debate adjourned.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Tomorrow as the first item we shall move to go into supply. When the motion is passed we shall call three departments, namely, external affairs, national defence and agriculture. Then we shall resume the' debate on the address. But from eight o'clock until nine there will be an hour for private and public bills.
I think there should be some explanation as to why it is felt that it is necessary to call three departments at this time. Why is it necessary to call more than one or at the most two at this time?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
At the beginning of any session since I have been in the house we never started off with one department; it was always with two or three. In this instance we are trying to meet the wishes of

the opposition who would like to have a day on some department. If I did not have three departments at my disposal, I would not undertake to get the ministers here at a time which would suit the opposition. I think this is a reasonable request to make for the start. As to next week, I shall have further discussions with the members of the opposition. I repeat that I want to co-operate. But on the other hand, there must be co-operation from both sides of the house. I really think that this request is reasonable.
I should think that two departments would be reasonable, because if one minister were away the other could bring forward his estimates.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext: He might be sick.

In any event, I would remind the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Fournier) that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) suggested that one department a week might be called. If three go through tonight, this must not be taken as a precedent that three or two should be called in subsequent weeks. This may be a comparatively long session; and as we know, when the departments are all in hon. members' opportunities for raising grievances in the house-the age-old custom -are limited. After what the Prime Minister said the other evening, I think we in the opposition must be careful that we do not allow too many departments to go in at this time lest we find ourselves in the position, a little later on, of not being able to raise grievances on going into supply, if we wish to do so, week by week, throughout the session, which may be a longer one than many of us anticipated when we came here.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
A long session, in my experience, is approximately twenty weeks. There are twenty or twenty-one departments that have to be brought in. Even if we bring in three departments today, and bring it up to about five, to give me a little leeway in the calling of departments, there will still be another fifteen or sixteen departments to be called. We could not go into supply on the first three days of the week without putting a formal motion. We have to have a formal motion even if we did not have any new departments to bring in. We could not study the estimates on a Monday, Tuesday
Business of the House
or Wednesday without putting a formal motion. Then hon. members can air their grievances.
Well, if I have not a certain number of departments, the order paper having very few bills, I would not like to take a chance of seeing the house without work in advance. The more that is considered the more it will be seen that I am quite reasonable.
All I am trying to do is to point out that it should not be regarded as a precedent for another week, or for subsequent weeks.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: We would not consider it in that way.

Because, after all, the house has set aside rules pretty thoroughly just lately. The very fact we are going into supply is against all parliamentary procedure until the house has voted confidence in the government. There is no question the house will vote that confidence; but custom is that this shall not be done until after the address has been approved, and, though the debate may be long or short, that is the procedure which the house should follow.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It will not be considered as a precedent. But I believe the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) would agree that, while government business is generally decided by the government, we never follow the rules strictly. Generally we consult with opposition leaders as to what would be the best procedure to follow. That is what we intend to do this year-not to keep to that strict rule whereby the government would just come in and announce its business and proceed in that way. I do not think that would go toward making progress.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Perhaps it was because the minister was interrupted, but I do not think he indicated what the business would be when and if we finish the matter of getting into supply.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I announced we would resume the debate on the address, with the exception of the hour from eight to nine, which goes to public and private bills.
It being five minutes after eleven o'clock, the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
